https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/arc.content:
Archives – August 13, 2020

During the last Triennale of Photography in Hamburg, I ran accross the photographer Katja Ruge during the opening at the Deichtorhallen. Apparently, she had recognized me over Instagram. Due to her great energy and radiant freshness, we kept in touch.

In 2019, I met her again during the big anniversary exhibition tour of the BFF – Berufsverband Freier Fotografen and Filmgestalter, I promoted in Stuttgart, Berlin and Hamburg. Her portrait of DJane VUUDUU became one of my favourite images inside the group show, and I started digging deeper into Ruge´s photographic world of photography (and music). The fusion of those two, seemingly aligned passions, but in fact two completely different worlds, has become the trademark of Katja Ruge´s art over the years. Like Olaf Heine and rock music, it’s the world of techno vibes & photography, which you see and feel in her portraits.

With an upcoming exhibition in Hamburg and her scheduled lecture during EMOP Berlin 2020 in October, I decided to meet with her and get to know more about “what’s new”.

Nadine Dinter:You are famous for your unique mix of “photography” and “music”. Explain us a little bit more about what this entails.

Katja Ruge:I`m a photographer, DJ, music producer and I run a party series for 10 years now.

The Love for Photography started when I learned in a photo lab. At the school we had to take our own photos. It just happened.Later I worked in a photo agency and my boss asked me if I go to all these concerts, take a camera.

First job was to do live photos of a Heavy Metal band at Markthalle Hamburg. I had no clue what I was doing but it was magic. I forgot space and time.

The combination of music and visuality drives me since them every day, every night.

When looking at your own photographs, how would you describe your trademark?

KR:Real People, Good Vibes. Something in-between. And lots of invisible lines.

Do you allow music during your photo shootings? Or is it even something to spice up the atmosphere and loosen up the people in front of your camera?

KR:I work a lot on location so most of the time its more the sound that surrounds us rather that setting up a boom box with good music.Often I ask people that I portrait to bring their fave music with them. I also have playlists on my Spotify with „photographic music“.I have a lack of concentration when the music takes off too much. It needs to be more background in a way that it melts into the photo session. I’m looking more for the flow. Then magic happens.

In your “first life”, you have worked as a photo assistant, then music promoter and art director, before starting our own business in 2000.

Which encounters/co-operations count among your favourite experiences during these years?

KR:Next to my job I always took photos and did assignments for magazines such as Der Spiegel, Manager Magazin or Allegra. It was mad but I needed the secure stuff till I finally said now let` s jump into being a full-time freelance photographer.Each job I did had its special experience which I don’t want to miss.

Music promotion I learned to care about artists, this reflects till today deeply in my way to work. I always want to have a good and creative atmosphere.

My work in one of the photo agency was insane. I saw every week new sessions of Herb Ritts, Wayne Maser, David LaChapelle, Mary Ellen Mark. Many iconic photographs in the 90s went over my desk. For seeing these photographs every day for a time period I’m extremely thankful, it shaped my understanding of image construction, positioning people and what makes a photo special.

In the 90s, you lived in Manchester, were deeply involved in the Rave-scene around the infamous Hacienda Club, and shot the highly regarded “Fotoreportage 23 l- In Search Of Ian Curtis”. Tell us a little bit about this project? How did the idea come up, where did you meet and how long did you work on this project?

KR:I lived in Manchester for around 2 1/2 years. I was lucky that I got in contact with Peter J. Walsh who was the staff photographer of the club Haçienda run by New Order and Tony Wilson / Factory Records. Peter worked there so I was there as well. Involved I must say no, but I was lucky to be there at the time. It was nuts and crazy. People partied like mad. Like you do when you’re young and there is all this great new music.It was all about that. I love when people are dedicated.

My photo project “Fotoreportage 23 – In Search Of Ian Curtis” I started in 2005, when I heard there will be a docu movie about Ian Curtis. I googled and found this list of places you have to visit as a JD fan and was intrigued. With the first help of my friend Gareth Davies, I met Mark Reeder in Berlin and my friend Tonie in Manchester drove me around. I started with the places and then later ask people to participate that had a connect to Ian. It was a hounting experience. And it became a book with photos on the cover of Ian Curtis shot by Mark Reeder. They were in a shelf hidden for over 25 years and I still can’t believe and are forever thankful I could use them for the book cover. Annik Honore organized the first exhibition in Brussels.

You have portrayed icons such as Björk, DJ Koze and rapper M.I. A. – how do you plan your shootings and how much liberty do you get in creating the vision you have in your mind?

KR:Most of the time planning is not possible. I’m the total expert in taking photos with what’s there and how is the mood of the artist in this moment (and mine, haha:) ).

I meet them in hotels or rooms of record companies. Mostly I try to go outside, if that’s not possible I look for a nice spot inside. Most of my sessions last only half an hour, I love this very concentrated energy.

When I do art direction as well and come up with a complete idea, location, stylist and make up/ hair it´s a beautiful process with mood-boards and listen to the artist music. That’s always my first connection and where I get ideas. Listen to DJ mixes and records. And if I need to decide and clear things I need to walk it out.

You are anofficial professional member of the renowned BFF – Berufsverband Freier Filmgestalter und Fotografen; which only has a few female members vs. the majority of male ones. Do you feel that female photographers are still encountering some kind of disadvantage or discrimination with regard to being booked for assigned work?

KR:As you know I have this photo project „Ladyflash – Women in Music“. It´s work in progress. I portrayed over 100 female musicians whether they are very famous or not. They have been exhibited all the same size to not focus through size of their fame. A lot of people asked me why I did it and not showing Peaches, Robyn, Janelle Monae or Beth Ditto bigger. I wanted complete equal rights. It starts with your own work. To answer your question; There is and will be disadvantage or discrimination for as long as we need to make such difference between people. Rich and Poor, Black and White, Women and Men. There is still a long way to go.

With the upcoming photography festival EMOP Berlin 2020, you will be presenting your work as part of the series “Meet the Pro”. Would you like to give us a little sneak preview?

KR:A lot of people who are not deeply routed in the music world don’t know my work so I’m gonna make a beautiful round trip through it. People will have the possibility to touch the photos, sit down and dive into it. The reaction when people actually can hold a photo is beautiful. And I have a little surprise too.

Your next show “One Room, One Light” will be openingat Tempel1844 Gallery in Hamburg, at the beginning of September. What is the project about?

KR:When the lockdown started gallery owner Thomas Holthoff in Hamburg who is doing this beautiful space send out via mail the opportunity to use it. Kind of a flat fallen out of time as an artist residency and space to create. It was part of the reform synagogue of the liberal New Israelite Temple Association in Hamburg, founded in 1817.

I immediately said I want to give local artists a space to come around and visit me, we take photos, eat, drink, talk, exchange.

Ended up doing also a session for RockCity e.V. a local supporter of the music scene run by amazing and ambitions women. The photos show several artists with slogan shirts to support them. The shirts are sold online and the money goes to struggling artists.

For the next generation of aspiring female photographers, what´s your advice?

KR:I noticed that a lot of women overthink too much. And look too much at others. I did in the past. It blocked me. When you get over it you start to find your true self. You do work that is real and full of Love.

It is great to find a mentor, somebody who helps you to grow as a person. This I find today more important than the latest skills in photography or a total perfect social media account.

Once I met Iris Apfel at the airport at Heathrow. I loved her coat so I told her. Without knowing who she was we had a great chat about being visible and “do your own thing no matter what people think”.And tried out face-balm at Boots Drugstore;)

Published by SKIRA, a curated selection of images retraces Bruce Gilden’s entire artistic journey, from his early black-and-white work to his recent colour photography.

A pioneer of street photography, and a full member of the Magnum Photos agency, Bruce Gilden (New York, 1946) is one of the undisputed protagonists of the international photography scene. His gaze penetrates the soul of the urban space and returns an immediate spectrum of situations, moods, and humanity, without filters or embellishments. While his early shots explore the city with a dynamic eye, among crowded sidewalks and hidden corners, his more recent work addresses issues such as vulnerability and marginalization, never succumbing to the aestheticization of pain. The photographer’s gaze rests on often invisible lives, producing striking images marked by a harsh, tragic, and deeply human beauty.

Gilden’s practice, defined by the photographer himself as in-your-face photography, is distinguished by a direct and radical language, able to capture the soul of his subjects and their relationship with their context.

Published on the occasion of the first monographic exhibition in Italy dedicated to the New York master of street photography, the book features a selection of approximately ninety images and centres on Faces (2013-2024), collecting portraits made as a figurative chronicle of cities around the world, from the United States to England, passing through Mexico, Greece, and Colombia. Alongside these, a series of black-and-white photographs of his beginnings (1968), taken in Japan (1996–1999), Haiti (1985–1995), Europe, but above all in his hometown, New York (1969–1995).

The book also features two new images inspired by the artworks by Raphael housed in the Pinacoteca Tosio Martinengo (The Angel and Christ Blessing), through which Gilden reinterprets the concept of “grace” expressed by the great Renaissance master.

Denis Curti is the artistic director of the Stanze della fotografia. From 2005 to 2014, he directed Contrasto-Milano. For more than fifteen years, he was the photographic critic for Vivimilano and Corriere della Sera, and he currently runs Black Camera on the Rolling Stone Italia digital platform. With Skira he recently published Joel Meyerowitz. A Sense of Wonder. Photographs 1962-2022 (2024).

Half a century ago, a legion of young idealists dropped out of society and went “back to the land,” creating a patchwork of utopian communes across Northern California.Handmade Utopia: Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern Californiatracks down the rogue souls still committed to this way of life, capturing their handbuilt, otherworldly residences alongside the stories of how they came to be—at what is now the tail end of one generation’s grand social experiment.Handmade Utopia travels the length of Northern California, which formed the epicenter of the movement, journeying down hidden dirt roads and deep into redwood forests to discover handmade homes kept hidden for decades. Michael Schmelling’s photography documents how these structures appear today and David Jacob Kramer’s oral histories detail how they came to be, and are presented alongside a plethora of archival materials.

In the mid-1960s, back-to-the-landers fled a Bay Area that had become over-policed and overrun with runaways, drugs and commercial exploitation. These new pioneers taught themselves to farm, practiced free love and generated radical new architectural styles. Only a fraction of these pioneers stuck it out for the decades following the Summer of Love. These flinty souls remain a study in principled self-reliance and human ingenuity. They are now in their 70s and 80s and the question arises of what they will leave behind, literally and figuratively. For decades they have kept these experimental homes hidden, long fearful of building inspectors and drug squads.Handmade Utopia presents these structures as artworks in their own right, captured at a moment when they risk being lost forever.

Handmade Utopia

Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern CaliforniaPhotographs by Michael Schmelling.

Edited with text and oral histories by David Jacob Kramer. Foreword by Jentri Anders.

Thierry Maindrault’s Monthly Cogitations

The summer months were the months of harvest , when hard work secured the economic future until the next cycle provided that everyone’s prayers to their gods brought favorable weather. Starting in the middle of the previous century, the story changed. Summer months were eagerly awaited to guarantee a well-deserved rest at least in theory and became a demand for time off during which the sun’s tanning rays became the common God. The future horizon, with its very material warnings, forces us to seriously reevaluate our intellectual approach. This imposes certain realities upon us that transform lazy lethargy into surges of stress, or even total anxiety for some. Thus, grueling labor has made a comeback—not to ensure bountiful harvests, but to limit all these unwelcome disasters.

What harrowing times our planet is presenting to us, a sort of wake-up call for our human “anthills.” All our modest plantations, our Pharaonic buildings, our defaced natural landscapes, are being swept away in a matter of seconds by water, fire, or wind. A return to a modicum of humility is in order by all those decision-makers whose supposedly great abilities have, unfortunately, worn out prematurely (to the very end) on the benches of prestigious schools for the elite.

Everything is catastrophic like the loss of a life that will remain etched in our memory. The material loss representing years of hard work will be a new challenge. The loss of memory forces us into a kind of wandering through our personal heritage.

None of us is immune to such an ordeal. I experienced the instant disappearance of my photographic artworks (several thousand photos) under a wave of mud in September 1992 (Vaison-la-Romaine). Such is the story of the universe, with its small human twist.

What truly struck me in the voyeuristic interviews of all the people who discovered their homes completely destroyed was the despair of those who, even though they had lost everything, clung to their photo albums. I was moved by the sense of relief expressed by those who said they had managed to save their photo albums. Everything was lost except the family’s soul this guiding thread of their heritage, preserved through a few photographs. This stood in stark contrast to those who were utterly devastated by the loss of their treasure trove of images. In every case, nothing remained of years of hard work and life; the very tangible difference in their suffering came down to a single photo album or box of photographs. Every lost or destroyed object causes dismay; a vanished image wounds the memory. Photography is the true witness that is passed down through the long generational relay.

It has been proven that photography has indeed become, through the intangible nature it expresses, the medium for heritage stories. It has become the legitimate descendant of cave engravings, ancient frescoes, and commissioned paintings. What matters is not the representation conveyed by the image; the essence lies in the spirit that springs from the album or escapes when the lid of the metal box is lifted. The emotional content is essential, given that the physical container is not always in great shape or is often quite worn out.

Since I’m on the subject of physical photography, I’ve noticed that when people talk about their treasures, in almost every case, they’re referring to photographs printed on paper. This makes sense for all photos taken before the advent of the multifunction smartphone. The phone stays in the pocket, the photos stay on the phone, and the risk of losing memories is close to zero. Yet, when a young intern journalist tried to reassure a young disaster victim that he’d been able to save many of his digital photos, he received this scathing response: “It’s not the same thing at all.” Let’s not confuse apples with oranges.

It seems clear that, for a few more years at least, authentic family photographs will be printed on paper. Whether they’re magnetized on the refrigerator, framed on the desk, or hung on a picture rail, these family images can be touched, carried around, and protected within the family’s cocoon. Certainly not in a phone, no matter how sophisticated it may be!

The final point we can address is the future of these images. Whether they remain within the family circle or scatter into other environments, their fate is often the same.

Firstly, it is not only disasters whether natural or accidental that can permanently erase an image, its context, its message, and the emotions it evokes. Stupidity, ignorance, fanaticism, and human anger are capable of destroying memories, shared experiences, and personal accounts. It is a fact, without comment: the past and future become invisible, just like most brains.

At the other extreme, the photographic image stands as one of the major assets of memory to be passed on to enrich our evolution. Our evolution, which is supposed to grow richer from one generation to the next. However, this choice to preserve requires a minimum organization to ensure the safekeeping and accessibility of the images. While there is no such thing as zero risk for a photograph any more than for anything else, basic precautions must be taken depending on the medium. Furthermore, being able to find the desired image in the right place at the right time remains a determining factor for the survival and transmission of this photographic memory.

Finally, there is the option of adding a personal modern twist to the memory of our ancestors. Generally, a paintbrush or pen is used, along with paint or ink, to make its mark on the weathered image. While the limited imagination of our pseudo-creatives may be interesting in theory, the reality is quite another matter. In far too many cases, our small-time “Leonardo da Vinci” feel compelled to butcher unique originals to satisfy their artistic urges. When it comes to destruction, landslides, fires, and floods have the merit of being real not exaggerated by a perverse ego. Nevertheless, for a creator who lacks technical mastery of photography but wishes to build upon the legacy of the past, the temptation to make a contribution may be justified. But in such cases, let’s respect the original work. It’s so easy to rework copies, especially since the message and its emotional impact will change if the “makeover” is successful. Why not add a literary touch to a photo of the grandparents’ wedding or a splash of acrylic paint to a photo of the Chinese exodus? But let’s preserve our originals and their credit (if it still exists).

What we call, somewhat pejoratively, the “family photo” is an important pillar of our photographic world. I would even go so far as to say that it is the one that generates the most emotion and sensuality even if the photograph is botched or poor.

It goes without saying that the involuntary loss of these photographic traces is always a form of intellectual and psychological heartbreak. The feeling of rage that grips every professional photographer upon the accidental loss of a work turns into despair when the destroyed image contains a part of the soul.

Thierry Maindrault –August 14, 2026

your comments about this chronicle and its photography are always welcome at

[chronicles@maindrault.art](mailto:chronicles@maindrault.art)

Image 57: Rencontres d'Arles 2026: Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias (2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. S'appuyant sur la photographie, la sculpture, l'intelligence artificielle et des archives familiales, ce projet explore ce que signifie se souvenir, oublier et prendre soin d'une personne dont le sentiment d'identité s'effrite progressivement. #arles #amanaman

Image 59: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 61: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 65: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 67: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 69: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 71: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Image 73: Portfolio: ‘Pacific Insomnia’ is an ongoing photographic series shot in French Polynesia. Every year, travelling funfairs stop off in Tahiti for a few weeks before moving on. For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

Image 75: Exhibition: Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. The International Center of Photography (ICP) presents Panjereh, an exhibition by Iranian-American artist Sheida Soleimani.Panjereh—which means ‘window’ or ‘passageway’ in Farsi—builds on Soleimani’s ongoing Ghostwriter series, in which she explores her parents’ experiences of political exile and migration as a lens to examine broader systems of geopolitics. Known for her intricate, studio-based compositions that combine photographs, props, live animals and even her own parents in surreal, magical realist scenes, Soleimani expands her practice in Panjereh with the debut of a new body of work featuring injured birds.

These images draw from her work as a wildlife rehabilitator and founder of Congress of the Birds, a federally licensed wild bird rehabilitation center in Rhode Island. The exhibition will also include a new site-speciﬁc wall drawing created speciﬁcally for ICP’s galleries.

Curated by Elisabeth Sherman, Guest Curator, the exhibition will bring together more than forty photographs, the vast majority of which have never before been shown in New York. Sherman states, “In her work, Soleimani uniquely braids together the complex particularities of her family’s history, deep research into geopolitics and her inherited passion for care work into a visual language completely her own. The magically inventive spaces she creates allow for complexity in telling these stories, honoring their richness and continually unfolding nature. It is truly an honor to be presenting her ﬁrst institutional solo exhibition in New York, speciﬁcally at an institution historically dedicated to photography that engages with the politics of our time.”

The Ghostwriter series takes Soleimani’s family history—speciﬁcally that of her parents’ ﬂight from Iran as political refugees following the 1979 revolution—as an overarching conceptual framework that informs her creative process, from the signiﬁcance of the objects and family ephemera she uses to the compositions of the photographs themselves. The series carries out a form of ‘ghostwriting’ in the way it both narrates and reconstructs the lives of Soleimani’s parents without utilizing their voices directly. The works focus on their lives in Iran as pro-democracy activists before then being forced to ﬂee the country, enduring both physical and psychological hardship on their way to eventual resettlement in the United States.

Soleimani’s mother was forced to give up being a practicing nurse, leading her to begin caring for wild birds, a skill which she would eventually pass along to her daughter.

With their personal emphasis, the Ghostwriter works present a distinct expression of Soleimani’s longstanding interest in Iranian history and the contemporary geopolitics between the West and the Middle East. Rather than address this history using a strictly documentary approach, Soleimani instead examines storytelling and memory as the primary means through which these stories are transmitted; the construction of her pictures captures the way that detail and meaning are often obscured, transformed or diﬃcult to fully grasp. This process is expressed by the degree of visual compression and accumulation of detail that Soleimani’s photographs contain, as speciﬁc passages, details or textures—wildlife and plants, architecture and landscape—regularly function as stand-ins and metaphors rather than straightforward description. Soleimani situates artifacts from her parents’ journey against backgrounds made up of imagery pulled from a variety of archival family photographs, resulting in works that are layered composites of multiple stories, documenting factual traces of history within newly imagined spaces.

A new development within the Ghostwriter series are the Flyways photographs, which draw attention to the plight of migratory birds, many of whom are wounded on their long journeys through populated areas. Soleimani’s work as a federally licensed wildlife rehabilitator grew out of a care practice that she learned from her mother and forms part of a larger cultural inheritance that has been passed down to her. Assuming the position of primary characters, the birds that Soleimani photographs and places within her tableaux provide a metaphor for the many social, political and environmental obstructions met by people forced into ﬂights of their own.

This new group of analog photographs that Soleimani made of rehabilitated birds presents a unique kind of maximalism despite their small scale while also forgoing the complex layering of reference and imagery typical of the Ghostwriter series. Shot in extreme close-up, these works render the bodies of birds as intensely detailed and complex worlds unto themselves, where feathers, talons and eyes are as richly described as Soleimani’s family history is explored. The acts of care contained within these images highlights the relationship between care and political resistance that has unfolded not only with Soleimani’s own family, but which remains critically important for our present moment.

About Sheida SoleimaniSheida Soleimani (b. 1990) is an Iranian-American artist, educator and activist. The daughter of political refugees who escaped Iran in the early 1980s, Soleimani makes work that excavates the histories of violence linking Iran, the United States and the Greater SWANA Region. In working across form and medium—especially photography, sculpture, collage and ﬁlm—she often appropriates source images from popular/digital media and resituates them within defamiliarizing tableaux. The composition depends on the question at hand. For example, how can one do justice to survivor testimony and to the survivors themselves (To Oblivion)? What are the connections between oil, corruption and human rights abuses among OPEC nations (Medium of Exchange)? How do nations work out reparations deals that often turn the ethics of historical injustice into playing ﬁelds for their own economic interests (Reparations Packages)? How may the layering of memory and familial history both report fact and produce a reckoning with the intimate resonances of a geopolitics of violence (Ghostwriter)? In contrast to Western news, which rarely covers these problems, Soleimani makes work that persuades spectators to address them directly and eﬀectively.

Soleimani’s work is held in permanent collections including the Guggenheim Museum, Museum of Fine Arts Boston, Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, MIT List Visual Art Center and Kadist Paris. Her work has been recognized internationally in both exhibitions and publications such as The New York Times, Financial Times, Art in America, Interview Magazine, and many others. Based in Providence, Rhode Island, Soleimani is also an Associate Professor of Studio Art at Brandeis University and a federally licensed wildlife rehabilitator.

Image 59: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 65: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 67: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 69: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 71: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/luc.content:
On the margins of everyday life, carousels occupy public squares. Illuminated by strings of light bulbs, they turn slowly. Their playful, mechanical, and nostalgic melodies repeat endlessly.

At the edge of this fleeting event, I set up my photographic device at a child’s eye level. The long exposure stretches movement and reveals a suspended sense of time. Photography strips the attraction of its immediacy, unveiling motion itself as it materializes on paper, frozen into fleeting sensations.

With each photograph, I summon the original carousel of my Milanese childhood, long vanished from both the city and my memory. Yet it persists, reappearing in other forms. The landscapes change, but the outlines remain the same.

Within the image, my memory takes shape without ever allowing itself to be fully grasped.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/bra.content:
Her multiple-exposure photographs are created by repeatedly exposing the same frame of film in different locations over time, allowing separate moments, places, and encounters to converge within a single image. Working in a manner akin to a magician, she uses the camera not simply as a recording device but as a tool for revealing relationships that ordinarily remain invisible. While the photographs are composed entirely of real places and events, the layering of exposures allows unseen connections, memories, energies, and patterns to manifest as imagined environments that could never be witnessed through ordinary perception alone. Existing between documentation and transformation, the works challenge the assumption that reality is limited to what appears before us in a single moment. Rather than fabricating a fictional world, they reveal one assembled from fragments of lived experience, suggesting that reality itself may be far more interconnected, fluid, and mysterious than we are conditioned to believe.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/pet.content:
Waiting for Palms

Waiting for Palms is a series of urban landscape photographs taken in Morocco and Egypt, which explores where the quiet traces of tradition intersect with the turbulence of modern expansion. The geography travels across central Morocco, from Essaouira to Marrakech, through the Atlas Mountains, into the arid stretches of Drâa-Tafilalet, and back over the mountains to the old medina of Fes; in Egypt it follows the train tracks along the Nile, from Cairo to Luxor to Aswan and back. The images linger on the everyday, set within monumental landscapes and constructed from an accumulation of small, inglorious moments. Together, they form a mosaic of worlds that are immediate and enigmatic, intimate yet always elusive, offering an experience of perpetual interpretation.

In Morocco, a false sense of timelessness at first seems to permeate the landscapes. Daily life in the medina of Marrakech does not bustle; instead, scooters and people seem to glide above the market floor in a quiet commerce, frozen by the photographs in an ubiquitous calm. In the deserts, solitary citadels rise along the roadside in uneventful silence, ancient and magnificent yet nondescript all at once. The villages and canyons of the Dades Valley feel emphatically empty, as in the image of a lone donkey, the seemingly sole inhabitant of an earthen mountain village. Yet within this harshness, life insists on its own interactions, fracturing the austerity through murals, fruit stands, and countless quotidian interventions that emerge like thoughts made manifest. These reveal a subtle interplay between permanence and transience, suggesting not an immortal place but one where time is not master, but instead a negotiable guest.

The Egyptian journey moves from Cairo’s cacophonous modernity to the temple-shadowed quiet of Aswan, unfolding as a palimpsest in which each era inscribes itself without fully erasing what preceded it. In Cairo, a billboard’s comical and watchful eyes gaze over a speeding motorbike on the expressway, while in a market corner cats gather against faded movie posters in small tableaux that hint at the city’s layered mythology. Moving south, urban density gives way to countryside, punctured by crossings where crowds gather in an orchestrated chaos, clamoring, unhurried yet urgent. Two women shop happily, their traditional dress a counterpoint to the plastic toys of modernity around them, while a restaurant’s modern domes nod to ancient Nubian architecture. All scenes which tempt the tropes of timelessness, returning the traveler to the same disregard of time that surrounds Morocco’s vignettes, where the eternal and the immediate coexist within a single frame. This persistence of the everyday within monumental landscapes emerges as a magnificence of countless small and unheroic moments.

To the photographer, so foreign to these worlds, capture becomes an act of provisional translation, an attempt to hold the poetics of space where gestures of privacy contrast with tradition and where stillness and motion create an unspoken choreography of the streets. The camera draws away one veil only to create another, turning the private language of seeing into something shareable yet transformed. Each viewer brings their own encounter to the image, so that a boy glancing back at his friend on a bicycle might equally belong to an alley in Luxor or a narrow street half a world away. Together these frozen vignettes form a tapestry of two places brought near not through understanding but through a common relevance that remains beyond translation, worlds that are immediate and enigmatic, intimate yet always elusive, holding the observer in patient suspension and perpetual interpretation.

The 4th Dimension

The 4th Dimension is a conceptual fine art photography series exploring time as emotion rather than measurement. Through surreal self-portraits, symbolic clocks, and layered visual storytelling, each image reflects a different relationship with time—memory, loss, healing, identity, hope, and mortality. Together, the series invites viewers to look beyond the clock and consider how time shapes not only our lives, but who we become.

Solar fiction – 2026

This photographic series was produced in Miami Beach, an iconic territory shaped by a seaside imaginary defined by its Art Deco architecture, palm trees, and colorful lifeguard towers.

Initially inspired by the aesthetics of postcards and vernacular photography from the 1950s, the project gradually moves away from these references to develop a more graphic and contemporary visual language. The setting becomes a space of lines, rhythms, and colors in which the body fully integrates itself.

Through deliberately tight framing, the work explores the formal relationships between architecture, the body, and objects. The straight lines of the lifeguard towers interact with the curves of the ball, a recurring motif that runs through the series as a visual thread. Through the verticality of its lines, the female body becomes a form in its own right, extending and reshaping the surrounding space.

The styling, composed of pastel-colored swimsuits and accessories, echoes the architectural palette and situates the images within an imaginary that is at once seaside-inspired, retro, and contemporary.

Created at dawn, the photographs capture a crisp and radiant light. Situated between fine art photography and editorial imagery, the series constructs a solar fiction in which architecture, body, and color come together to create a graphic landscape illuminated by light.

The series received an Honorable Mention in the Fashion and Beauty category of the FotoSlovo International Photography Awards in 2026.

Tumultuous Skies

My photographs and videos are often inspired by the work of Alfred Stieglitz where the sky is the protagonist and the shapes of the clouds appear as if in a mirror of lights. This series was shot in Milan and Gavorrano, a small town in Tuscany. The sense of smallness in the face of the infinity of the sky is a romantic characteristic that I bring to my work. As in front of a painting, the attempt is to recover sensations of beauty and contemplation in front of the immensity of nature.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/mic.content:
Magical Delta

‘Magical Delta’ is an ongoing photographic project that documents deltas as fragile ecosystems, through a deliberate methodological framework: analogue photography guided by my neurodivergent perspective.

This combination is my own system of protection for the future of these ecosystems. Analogue negatives contain no metadata. The neurodivergent view, in perceiving and representing the landscape, generates images that are unreadable to geolocation algorithms. The result is my activist practice: images that reveal the magic of a place whilst protecting it from algorithmic identification, which accelerates uncontrolled tourism and environmental degradation. What I photograph of the delta is real, and it is a kind of magic that algorithms cannot recognise.

In the delta, conventional categories dissolve. Sky and earth, fresh and salt water, life and decay merge into landscapes where nothing is fixed or immobile. My neurodivergent perception does not correct this instability; it inhabits it, producing representations of the territory faithful to its nature rather than to rigid neurotypical thinking.

The project operates at the intersection of environmental concern, photographic materiality and non-normative epistemology. It asks what role the analogue medium can play—not as nostalgia, but as a future-oriented tool—in the protection of ecosystems that we are still learning to see.

What we choose not to see today shapes the worlds we inherit tomorrow.

Daniel Malikyar: Reclaiming the right to look

There are countries that history has ultimately reduced to images. Afghanistan is one of them. War, the Taliban, exile, ruins: over the decades, the Western gaze has produced such a powerful visual repertoire that it has come to stand in for the territory itself. It is precisely within this visually saturated space, that Daniel Malikyar chooses to work. Not to manufacture another image of Afghanistan more seductive or more consensual but to shift the very lines through which it is perceived. Afghan-American, born into the migratory history of his parents, Daniel Malikyar has a singular relationship with Afghanistan: it is a country that belongs to him intimately, while for a long time given to him from a distance. This position of in-betweenness is essential to his photography. It allows him to escape both the purely external gaze of the passing photographer and the illusion of a perfectly homogeneous sense of belonging. His lens occupies that uncertain space where family memory encounters direct experience, where the intimate becomes documentary material. His images therefore reject the urgency that so often characterizes photography devoted to territories in crisis. They take their time. They look at faces, bodies, landscapes, clothing, ordinary gestures. They bring back into the photographic field what geopolitical narratives tend to erase: the banality of being alive. The subject is no longer “Afghanistan” as a political abstraction, but Afghans in all their plurality, dignity, everydayness, and sometimes quiet beauty. This approach is all the more compelling because Malikyar also comes from a world in which images are traditionally associated with the construction of desire. As a photographer, filmmaker, and art director, he has developed a visual grammar shaped by advertising, music, and popular culture. His images therefore possess an unapologetically sophisticated formal precision: with carefully constructed compositions, an acute sensitivity to light, chromatic intensity, and a strong sense of framing. Yet where commercial imagery generally seeks to seduce, Malikyar uses this mastery to restore visibility where the gaze has grown accustomed to no longer seeing. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his work lies. Moving between documentary photography, cinema, and editorial language, he does not attempt to conceal the construction of the image. He embraces it. Because every photograph is already a choice, a frame, an interpretation. To show differently does not mean claiming a more objective truth; it means acknowledging that images themselves participate in the way we construct our understanding of the world.

With Afghanistan, his most personal project to date, Daniel Malikyar undertakes a form of visual reclamation. He photographs a country that is not only the land of his origins, but also the bearer of a collective memory he inherited without ever having fully experienced it. His images become fragments of a narrative searching for itself between transmission and experience, between nostalgia and the present, between belonging and distance. There is, ultimately, something in this approach that extends beyond the Afghan questions alone. What does it mean to photograph a country when it already exists in the world’s imagination before the shutter is even released? And how can one create images that do not simply replace one cliché with another, but restore to reality its density, contradictions, and unpredictability? Daniel Malikyar may not claim to answer these questions. He prefers to leave them open. And that is precisely what gives his work its resonance: behind the desire to show another Afghanistan lies a broader reflection on the power of images—on what they reveal, what they silence, and on the possibility, at times, of reclaiming one’s own narrative through photography.

Website : www.danielmalikyar.shop

Instagram : @dmalikyar

Current project:Afghanistan, a 240-page book published by teNeues / Die Gestalten Verlag. It is the first major photography book dedicated to Daniel Malikyar’s personal project, which he has been pursuing for several years in his country of origin. The book brings together more than 130 color photographs, accompanied by texts and personal narratives.

Your first photographic trigger?Daniel Malikyar: Curiosity sparked by my grandfather, Omar. Every year he would fly from Virginia to visit my family in Los Angeles, documenting our time together on film. After returning home, he would have the rolls developed and mail the photographs back to us, allowing me to relive those memories long after he had left.

A photographic memory from your childhood?

Daniel Malikyar: A printed photograph of the Buddhas of Bamiyan pinned to the roof of my father’s Chevrolet Astro that I would gaze at on the way to and from school every morning.

The camera of your childhood?Daniel Malikyar: A 35mm Canon Elph point-and-shoot.

The one you use today?Daniel Malikyar: A Fujifilm GFX100 II.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you?Daniel Malikyar: Sabrina and Roland Michaud, the French photographer couple who documented Afghanistan during a time of peace throughout the 1960s and 70s. Their photographs revealed a side of the country that felt almost absent from everything else I had seen growing up, reminding me there was so much more to Afghanistan’s story.

The image you wish you had taken?Daniel Malikyar: The photograph of the Brazilian national team’s locker room after winning the 2002 FIFA World Cup Final… even though I was only seven years old.

The one that moved you the most?Daniel Malikyar: A photograph of my parents on their wedding night. Rediscovering it while working on my Afghanistan project was incredibly emotional. Today, it’s reproduced at the end of my book.

And the one that made you angry?Daniel Malikyar: Nothing immediately comes to mind.

Which photograph changed the world?Daniel Malikyar: Nick Ut’s photograph The Terror of War from the Vietnam War. It helped open the world’s eyes to the devastating impact of conflict on innocent people caught in the crossfire.

And which photograph changed your world?Daniel Malikyar: A photograph I made of Noor Ali, a young boy flying a kite from his rooftop overlooking Kabul at sunrise. The image felt like the manifestation of the daydreams I had as a child after reading The Kite Runner and imagining what Afghanistan looked like beyond the headlines. It still sparks the question,what if? What if my life had been completely different? What if I had grown up in Afghanistan? It’s a photograph that carries a great deal of weight for me and one that transports me back to that morning every time I look at it.

A key image in your personal pantheonDaniel Malikyar: A photograph I made of two balloon sellers cycling through the streets of Kabul early one morning, captured serendipitously through the window of a taxi.

What interests you most in an image?Daniel Malikyar: Subject matter that tells a story and sparks curiosity.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object?Daniel Malikyar: Whether it asks more questions than it answers.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretative.” Do you agree?Daniel Malikyar: Yes, I agree with the sentiment. Black and white gives the viewer more room to interpret and explore because stripping away color creates a response driven more by imagination.

In your opinion, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography?Daniel Malikyar: I don’t think technique should take precedence, but I do think there are instances where it’s necessary to help convey emotion.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic?Daniel Malikyar: The most powerful beauty in photography, for me, is found through the story.

What elements can make silence visible in a photograph?Daniel Malikyar: Motion, light, shadow, color, texture, and eye contact.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Can a photograph be truer than reality?Daniel Malikyar: I believe the best photographs are not taken, they’re presented to you. Moments that can never be staged or replicated, disappearing almost as quickly as they reveal themselves. In those moments, a truth beyond reality can reveal itself in a way that almost feels magical.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event?Daniel Malikyar: Absolutely. Photography has the power to change, shift, and shape perspective. It’s for that reason that photographers carry such a great responsibility.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation?Daniel Malikyar: It can be both. The camera is simply a tool. It can be used to witness and document truth, or to create a carefully constructed interpretation of it.

What makes a good photograph?Daniel Malikyar: You notice something new every time you look at it.

In your opinion, what quality is necessary to be a good photographer?Daniel Malikyar: Humility. People can sense your intentions long before they notice your photographs.

How do you choose your projects?Daniel Malikyar: My work is inspired by my own lived experiences. Rather than seeking out events, I’m drawn to everyday life and revealing the extraordinary hidden within the ordinary.

How would you describe your creative process?Daniel Malikyar: 360-degree storytelling. The authentic alignment of personal connection, photographs, films, writing, artifacts, and lived experiences, all connected by a clear mission to celebrate the beauty of humanity through visual storytelling.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart?Daniel Malikyar: My Afghanistan project, which consists of a photography book published by teNeues, a documentary series with each episode corresponding to a chapter in the book, and a fine art exhibition featuring limited edition framed prints, projected films, and handcrafted artifacts. A percentage of all proceeds supports my nonprofit, which is dedicated to developing a community of Afghan visual storytellers by providing mentorship, equipment, funding, and the resources needed for Afghans to tell their own stories through their own perspectives.

The person you would like to photograph?Daniel Malikyar: Ronaldinho Gaúcho.

The person by whom you would like to be photographed?Daniel Malikyar: My grandfather, Omar. May he rest in peace.

An essential photography book?Daniel Malikyar: Football Roots by my friend Sam Robles.

What is the last photograph you took?Daniel Malikyar: A portrait of my mom over lunch about an hour ago, moments after showing her the first physical copy of my book. A special moment.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook, TikTok — and why?Daniel Malikyar: Instagram. I still think it’s the platform best suited for visual storytelling.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media?Daniel Malikyar: An inundation of repetition.

An Instagram account everyone should follow?Daniel Malikyar: @whatsculture

What is your view on AI?Daniel Malikyar: It’s a complicated topic. But I don’t believe anything can substitute real human stories. My work will always focus on shining a light on people, often in communities and places that have gone unseen.

Color or black and white?Daniel Malikyar: Color.

Natural light or artificial light?Daniel Malikyar: Natural light.

Which city seems the most photogenic to you?Daniel Malikyar: Havana, Cuba.

The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering?Daniel Malikyar: While I’ve traveled across much of Afghanistan, there’s still so much left to discover. I can’t wait to continue exploring it.

A place you never tire of?Daniel Malikyar: Afghanistan’s Wakhan Corridor. The most peaceful place I’ve ever visited.

The image that, for you, represents the current state of the world?Daniel Malikyar: I don’t think a single image comes to mind.

In your opinion, what is missing in today’s world?Daniel Malikyar: The understanding that we’re far more similar than we are different. I hope my Afghanistan project serves as a reminder of that. It’s important that we celebrate the cultural nuances that make us unique rather than allow them to become reasons for division.

If God existed, would you ask Him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie with Him?Daniel Malikyar: I would opt to create a portrait.

Your favorite drug?Daniel Malikyar: The feeling of waking up in a new place for the first time with no expectations other than experiencing it with an acute sense of presence.

Your best way to disconnect?Daniel Malikyar: With a football at my feet.

Your latest madness?Daniel Malikyar: I’ve been on the road nonstop for the last two years, so my tolerance for madness is fairly high. But maybe I’d say witnessing Cabo Verde’s equalizer against Argentina in extra time of the World Cup at three in the morning in Paris, and recognizing the weight and importance of what that moment represented for underdogs around the world.

Your greatest professional extravagance?Daniel Malikyar: Closing the lease on my apartment, putting everything I owned into a storage unit, and buying a one-way ticket to Afghanistan to document the unseen human stories and celebrate the beauty of its people, places, and culture. Along the way I often slept on strangers’ floors and spent days traveling off-road to reach villages that had never seen a camera before.

A profession you would not have liked to pursue?Daniel Malikyar: One that involves no natural light.

Which question unsettles you the most?Nothing comes to mind.

The last thing you did for the first time?Daniel Malikyar: Just a few days ago, I was walking the streets of the smallest municipality in Italy when I was invited into an Italian grandparents’ home to share homemade cake and a conversation that blended Italian, Spanish, English, and Google Translate. It was a beautiful reminder of what travel can be, and the kind of experience I hope continues to find me.

Your greatest regret?Daniel Malikyar: Not archiving all of my personal photographs growing up before hard drives and the cloud became readily accessible.

If you had to start all over again?Daniel Malikyar: We’re just getting started.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be at the table?Daniel Malikyar: My parents and my best childhood friends, eating by the Mediterranean Sea at sunset during the summer.

What do you like people to say about you… after you’re gone?Daniel Malikyar: That my presence created a positive impact.

The one thing people absolutely must know about you?Daniel Malikyar: That I always do everything in my power to fulfill what I say I’m going to do. Keeping my promises means everything to me.

A final word?Daniel Malikyar: Thank you for having me.

All About Photo presents David Saxe : Cuba es Vida, a deeply personal photographic journey through shadow, movement, and the enduring spirit of the Cuban people.

Cuba has long inspired photographers with its vibrant streets, colorful architecture, and unmistakable atmosphere. In Cuba es Vida, David Saxe looks beyond these familiar images to reveal a more personal and nuanced portrait of the island. Created over the course of three journeys, the project explores the rhythms of everyday life, where history, resilience, and human connection quietly unfold.

Rather than documenting Cuba’s iconic landmarks, Saxe is drawn to its people and the moments that often go unnoticed. Musicians rehearsing in empty theaters, fishermen preparing their boats at dawn, children training in boxing gyms and ballet schools, and elderly residents reflecting on lives shaped by history become the heart of the story. His photographs celebrate ordinary life while revealing the remarkable spirit that continues to define the country.

What distinguishes Cuba es Vida is its visual language. Saxe embraces darkness, blur, and atmosphere, allowing emotion to take precedence over description. His photographs resist the polished perfection often associated with travel photography. Instead, shadows soften the edges of memory, movement suggests the pulse of daily life, and imperfect moments become powerful expressions of authenticity. The result is a body of work that feels both intimate and timeless.

Throughout the series, Cuba emerges as a place where past and present exist simultaneously. Colonial architecture slowly fades, political history remains visible, and the marks of time appear everywhere. Yet these changes never overshadow the warmth, resilience, and generosity of the Cuban people. Saxe’s photographs acknowledge the country’s complexities while remaining deeply rooted in its humanity.

For Saxe, the true story of Cuba lies not in its famous streets or classic cars, but in its gestures, conversations, music, and shared moments. His images invite viewers to experience the country emotionally rather than simply observe it, offering a perspective that moves beyond familiar visual clichés.

With Cuba es Vida, David Saxe presents a thoughtful and evocative portrait of contemporary Cuba—one that favors atmosphere over spectacle and feeling over documentation. His photographs remind us that the essence of a place is often found not in its landmarks, but in the people who continue to give it life.

About David Saxe

Born in Montreal, Québec, Canada, in 1943, David Saxe studied fine art at l’École des Beaux-Arts in Montreal. His interest in photography was sparked by the work of Robert Frank, Roy DeCarava, and Henri Cartier-Bresson.

For four years, he studied under renowned Canadian photographer John Max and participated in numerous group and solo exhibitions throughout Canada before moving to the United States in 1992. Today, Saxe divides his time between San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, and Santa Fe, New Mexico.

Galerie Iso presents De la lumière à l’empreinte by Thierry Valencin.

Photography came to Thierry Valencin and carved within him a pure space that pierces the sparks of shadow.

The photographer invites us into a territory where photography no longer settles for capturing reality

His images resonate with a power that is both popular and poetic.

With De la lumière à l’empreinte, he continues a body of research deeply attached to photographic matter. Between sharpness and blur, presence and absence, his images question what remains once the gaze has already begun to drift away.

This exhibition finds its natural place at Galerie Iso, founded in 2015 by Delphine Bonnet, Thierry Valencin, and Bernard Minier. The gallery champions an auteur-driven photography rooted in black and white and analog practice.

The gallery is currently showing prints by Denis Brihat, Jean Claude Gautrand, and Hans Silvester.

Exhibition until October 4, 2026

Image 63: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 71: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Archives – August 17, 2022

You can enjoy the magic of the landscapes of Tuscany, but an attractive destination for those who are keen on photography is located right in the heart of the region. Indeed, the 12 th edition of the international photography festival Cortona On The Move, focusing on Me, Myself and Eye: The Intimate Relationship Between Photography, Society and Identity is on until October 2, with dozens of exhibitions, talks, portfolio reviews, conferences and workshops.

Painted or engraved, images have always played an important role in society, even in very ancient cultures such as the Etruscan one (and Cortona in the 4th-5th century B.C.was one of the most prosperous Etruscan cities). So it can be the ideal place for debating on photography as a full-featured language.

The pervasiveness of photography in our contemporary world is a matter of fact. According to the artistic director Paolo Woods, “at this crucial moment, when photography is more relevant than ever and has become a universal language –produced, shared and consumed in a ravenous manner– Cortona On The Move comes to reflect on authorship, point of view and legitimacy, on how subject and object intersect, collide and finally coexist”.

The festival’s 12th edition is reflecting on photography as a full-fledged language, as already foretold since the very beginning of this media. As this year’s theme is inspired by the title of one of Billie Holiday’s ballads, ‘Me, Myself and I’, Paolo Woods hopes that ”viewers can question how photography is never absolute, but rather acquires different meanings depending on who produces and who consumes it”

“In 2022, Cortona On The Move goes on with its research into the contemporary documentary narration and the evolution of the photographic medium in order to let it accessible to the general public, thus making it a catalyst for exchange and cultural growth ” Veronica Nicolardi, director of the festival, adds.

The debate is on the grammar of this very language as well as on its rules, starting from the following: Who has the right to photograph what? Maybe you cannot find a definitive answer but observing the works by internationally known photographers can offer interesting ideas.

Martin Parr & The Anonymous Project (Déjà View. A Conversation in Colour), Jacob Holdt(American Pictures – I Just Do Things), Stacy Kranitz (As it was Give(n) to Me), Alessandro Cinque (Ser y aparecer),

Walter Niedermayr (Transformations / Dialogue between self and space), Jan Banning (The Sweating Subject), Lucas Foglia (Constant Bloom) are among the authors displaying their works.

Other exhibitions are connected with the AlUla Arts Festival, like Fast–Paced by Hayat Osamah or Wrinkles by Hussain Alsumayen. There is also a section on Stories of Humanity. Photographers for Doctors Without Borders (MSF), with works such as There are crocodiles in the sea by Filippo Taddei or RIP: Rest In Pieces by Giuliano Lo Re.

Without forgetting the prizes awarded during the festival, like the Cortona On The Move Award, the first edition of the festival’s open call, that is part of the constant search for original and innovative narratives that have always characterized the event. Zed Nelson, Rima Maroun e Gleeson Paulino are the winners of the COTM Award. Nicolò Filippo Rosso with Exodus, instead, is the winner of the Premio Ponchielli 2022, in collaboration with GRIN (Gruppo Redattori Iconografici Nazionale)

The exhibitions and the events are on display in the town’s historic centre, the Medici Fortress of Girifalco, and the new ‘Station C’ location near the Camucia-Cortona Station. The Cortona On The Move festival, organised by ONTHEMOVE cultural association, is under the patronage of the Region of Tuscany and the Municipality of Cortona.

Paola Sammartano

Paola Sammartano is a journalist, specialized in arts and photography, based in Milan.
