https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/the.content:
Gad Edery: The Collector’s Eye

From finance to photography, Gad Edery did not change worlds; he changed his way of seeing. For fifteen years, between Paris, Geneva and London, he worked in the trading world. Yet along his career, another, more personal story was taking shape: that of a collector who began acquiring artworks at the age of 19 and developed a particular passion for photography. In London, from 1997 onwards, he discovered a medium whose market was still in its infancy, and whose major works were, at the time, still within reach. This encounter would gradually become a conviction. In 2008, as the financial crisis profoundly disrupted the world in which he had worked, Gad Edery left the markets to devote himself entirely to what had, until then, been a passion. He founded GADCOLLECTION, a gallery entirely devoted to photography. The choice was far from incidental. His aim was not simply to follow an emerging market, but to champion a medium he believed was still largely underestimated one capable of bringing together artistic rigor, history and accessibility. His vision as a gallerist is deeply informed by his experience as a collector. GADCOLLECTION was built around a simple yet ambitious idea: to bring important photographers back into the spotlight, including those who have sometimes remained outside the speculative mechanisms of the market, while also making room for younger artists when the quality of their work warrants it. The gallery thus brings together historical photography, contemporary practice, portraiture, fashion, landscape, fine-art photography, astrophotography and even NASA archives. This diversity, however, is anything but a lack of focus. On the contrary, it reveals a distinctly personal understanding of photography: an image may be documentary, spectacular, conceptual, iconic or intimate, provided it possesses that rare ability to make an impression on the viewer that endure.. For Gad Edery, the role of the gallerist is therefore as much about selecting as it is about transmitting. Advising a collector, guiding a first acquisition, bringing an artist back into the spotlight, telling the history of photography through works of art: his work is almost as much about education as it is about commerce. This approach also explains the dialogues his exhibitions regularly seek to create between generations. In 2026, the exhibition Dialogue, devoted to Markus Klinko, brought the photographer’s work into conversation with figures such as William Helburn and Jean-Daniel Lorieux, revealing connections around fashion, glamour, the construction of desire and the image’s fictional power. At a time when photography occupies an increasingly important place in collections and on the art market, Gad Edery continues to defend a singular position: that of a gallerist who prides himself of his collector’s eye, values quality above market price, and considers photography not simply as a commodity, but as a way of looking at the world and, sometimes, of dreaming it. Meet the gallerist whose journey also reflects the evolving status of photography within contemporary art.

Site web: www.gadcollection.comInstagram: @galeriegadcollection

What was your first photographic revelation?Gad Edery:99 Cents by Gursky.

A photographic memory from your childhood?Gad Edery: Family photo albums and holiday slide shows.

The camera of your childhood?Gad Edery: A Kodak Instamatic that made a metallic sound when you wound the film!

The one you use today?Gad Edery: My smartphone.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you?Gad Edery: Difficult to say, but I have a passion for space photography. Otherwise, I really like the work of Luigi Ghirri.

The image you wish you had taken?Gad Edery: Photographing Neil Armstrong on the Moon. I would have loved to be an astronaut.

The one that moved you the most?Gad Edery: There are two. The first is a photograph by Henryk Ross, taken in the Łódź Ghetto: a mother kissing her child. The second is a photograph by Nobuyoshi Araki a portrait of his wife in her bath.

And the one that made you angry?Gad Edery: None.

Which photograph changed the world?Gad Edery: The photograph of Neil Armstrong on the Moon. The possibility of another world.

And which photograph changed your world?Gad Edery: The same one! If humankind was able to go to the Moon, then nothing is impossible.

A key image in your personal pantheon?Gad Edery: I live surrounded by images, so that’s a difficult question. Some have greater significance than others. That is the case with a photograph by Florence Chevallier from the series Enchantements, 1, 1996. Buzz Aldrin’s self-portrait in space during the Gemini 12 mission, in November 1966, and Bruce McCandless’s photograph from February 1984 are also important to me.

As a gallerist, what interests you most in an image?Gad Edery: What interests me most is that an image should have a direct message. An image a statement. I don’t understand images that require an explanation to grasp what the artist intended to say. I find that a waste of time. The artist would have been better off being a writer.

In your view, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography?Gad Edery: Under no circumstances.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic?Gad Edery: Beauty is a volatile and subjective notion. It can reveal itself in many ways, aesthetics being one of them, but not the only one.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from the staging?Gad Edery: It can come from both. It all depends on the photographer’s intention.

Can a photograph be more truthful than reality?Gad Edery: Photography is the capture of a moment in reality. Reality is malleable, but in my view, it cannot be more truthful than the object being photographed.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event?Gad Edery: Yes, without a doubt. That is actually one of the dangers of photography. What we see is not always the truth. The advent of artificial intelligence will only increase this possible distortion between the reality of an event and what we are shown.

Is photography a form of testimony or a form of manipulation?Gad Edery: Photography can be both: a testimony and a lie.

What makes a good photograph?Gad Edery: A perfect alignment between what is looked at and the person looking.

In your opinion, what quality is essential to being a good photographer?Gad Edery: As in many things: curiosity and patience.

How do you choose the artists you work with?Gad Edery: It often comes down to human encounters. First, the body of work needs to be coherent and structured. Then, I need to want to champion the artist’s work over the long term. Finally, I need to want to have the artist’s photographs at home and live with them.

The person you would like to photograph?Gad Edery: Sadly, I have no talent as a photographer! I think I’m like everyone else: I enjoy photographing the people close to me and everyday situations.

The person you would like to be photographed by?Gad Edery: Strangely enough, despite representing renowned photographers, some of whom have been kind enough to photograph me, I have very few photographs of myself.

That said, I had the good fortune to exhibit one of the greatest portrait photographers there is: Stéphane de Bourgies. His black-and-white portraits are extraordinary. I hope he will want to photograph me!

An essential photography book?Gad Edery: Yes, there is one essential book to read, but it isn’t a photography book! It is The Story of Art by Ernst Gombrich. Surely one of the most important art historians, who manages to make sometimes rather complex concepts accessible to everyone.

What is the last photograph you took?Gad Edery: I use my smartphone a lot as a notebook. So I take plenty of photographs and screenshots of things that interest me. Otherwise, the last personal one was a photograph with one of my oldest friends, who came to visit me in Paris this weekend.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok — and why?Gad Edery: I only use social media for my professional activities (Galerie GADCOLLECTION / In Gad We Trust.Art / Musée de la Photographie.com). For everything else, I’m fortunate enough to have a rich personal life.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media?Gad Edery: Everyone thinks they’re a photographer! That said, if it makes people happy, why not!

An Instagram account that absolutely must be followed?Gad Edery: Whichever one interests you most! And if it’s the gallery’s, even better!

What is your view of AI?Gad Edery: A wonderful technological invention that raises very real ethical questions. The advantage of technology is that, in order to exist, it needs electricity. We can always unplug it!

Color or black and white?Gad Edery: Why should we have to choose when we can have both!

Natural or artificial light?Gad Edery: Both!

Which city strikes you as the most photogenic?Gad Edery: There isn’t one in particular.

The place you never tire of?Gad Edery: The desert.

The image that, for you, represents the current state of the world?Gad Edery: Joker! But I tend to see the bright side of things.

If God existed, would you ask Him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie with Him?Gad Edery: I’d ask Him to pose for me! It’s not every day you get to give God instructions!

Your favorite drug?Gad Edery: I’m fortunate enough to love my work and to work a great deal. So, my work. But I also love doing nothing and wandering around! Even when I’m not “doing” anything, there’s always something work-related going on in my head!

Your best way to disconnect?Gad Edery: Traveling and reading.

Your greatest regret?Gad Edery: I don’t think I have one.

If you had to start all over again?Gad Edery: I’ve been lucky enough to have a very eclectic life, with very different horizons. That said, probably the same thing—but I would have loved to be an astronaut, an adventurer, a writer, a chef, a conductor, an industrialist, a real-estate developer, and surely many other things!

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be at the table?Gad Edery: The people I love and with whom I’m lucky enough to share my life. Some I’ve known since kindergarten, others I’ve met more recently.

One last word?Gad Edery: See you soon at the gallery!

Text and interview by Carole Schmitz

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/ski.content:
SKIRA publishes Pablo Arroyo : Plates, The first monograph dedicated to Pablo Arroyo’s new professional project, a return to “pure” and essential photography.

After years devoted to fashion photography for the most prestigious international brands, Pablo Arroyo presents a new and significant chapter in his professional career, which consciously goes “beyond” the boundaries of fashion photography. It is a choice that breaks with the past and, at the same time, marks a return to the origins: a renewed closeness to “pure” photography.

The artist’s gaze becomes more intimate and rigorous, focusing on the essence of the subjects and the intrinsic power of the image. His photographs are characterised by an essential, direct visual language, free of embellishment, in which objects and nudes emerge forcefully from the background, isolated and laid bare in their formal and expressive uniqueness.

Creative, art director, and photographer, Pablo Arroyo (Mexico City, 1975) is a leading figure in the contemporary landscape of photography and creative direction. His education is rooted in studies of art history, screen printing, and engraving in Mexico, and was later consolidated in Italy, where he moved in the early 1990s to pursue graphic design, photography, and art history at the Istituto Europeo di Design in Milan.

After an initial experience as a graphic designer at Vogue Italia, Arroyo began a full-time career as a photographer in 1998, collaborating with numerous Italian and international magazines and producing catalogues and campaigns for major fashion houses, including Alexander McQueen, Gucci, Trussardi, and Valentino.

In 2009, he launched his first independent magazine/project in Paris, marking the beginning of a path increasingly focused on creative direction and the development of brand visual identities. In parallel, he held prominent editorial roles as Creative Director and Editor in Chief of L’Officiel Hommes Italia (2011–2015) and L’Officiel Hommes Paris (2015–2019). With Skira Pablo Arroyo recently published Panorama of Contemporary Italian Fashion Photography (2024).

“I invent nothing. I imagine everything. I have sought only to express reality, for nothing is more surreal” – Brassaï.

Walk with me through a foggy Parisian night. Pause. Watch the mist fall in gentle swirls wrapping the city in gossamer folds. Feel the damp upon your skin. Wander the streets in the liminal space between dusk and dawn. Meander along the banks of the River Seine lulled by the slapping of water on the shore, the flutter of falling leaves. Linger between dream and reality. Play in the light and shade. Look in ways you have not seen before. Wonder at the extraordinary of the quotidian. Pay homage to lives now long passed. The echo of a memory, revealing itself anew.

One of the most alluring aspects of the photograph is its capacity to transport the viewer to another world, to take us beyond what we know or to remind us of what we have forgotten. Nearly a century after Brassaï’s Secret Paris photographs were taken, they continue to fascinate. Compelling, rich with narrative and exuding the humanist qualities that underpinned this artist’s work, Brassaï’s photographs are undoubtedly some of the most arresting pictures of all time.

Entering the Brassaï’s Secret Paris exhibition at the Heide Museum of Modern Art (Melbourne) is to arrive at another time and place. Brassaï’s deep, emotional connection to the images he created, first in his mind and then on glass plates and as prints, are enthralling and profound. Each represents a moment, a life suspended in time, which for me encapsulates the enduring value of the medium. Yet these photographs transcend the notion of documentation, conveying a level of intimacy that is possible because of Brassaï’s ability to reach beyond the superficial and take us with him into his world.

To say I love Brassaï’s Secret Paris is to underplay the connection I feel to the ‘luminous years’ in which this polymath found his way to photography allowing generations to experience one of the world’s greatest cities in all its guises through his unique way of looking. To know Brassaï’s photography is to understand the difference between seeing and looking, and to meet in that place where intellect and imagination collide with reality. Brassaï’s photography forces you to give yourself up to what’s happening in the image and unprompted, let it do its magic. I have long admired Brassaï’s work, read his letters to his parents during the early years when he was struggling in Paris and spent time with his images. The Heide show is the first time I have stood amongst the vintage prints that Brassaï made in his “laboratoire” (darkroom) and it is a spine-tingling moment.

In 1899 Gyula Halász was born in the small Hungarian Transylvania town of Brassó. After studying fine arts in Budapest and Berlin, and serving in the military, in 1924 at the age of 25, he moved to Paris where he spent the rest of his life. It was at this time he adopted the name Brassaï. An artist who used a range of materials to convey his ideas, from writing and sculpture to photography, Brassaï is best known for the latter, a medium he embraced to express his insatiable curiosity about the human condition.

However, being a polymath comes with its own preoccupations and Brassaï longed for artistic freedom, writing that he would have liked to model himself in “the tradition of the seventeenth-century humanists, that is, those great figures of the Renaissance who were granted the right to develop, in harmony, all their talents in life and in the arts including thinking.” Brassaï lamented that “specialization, one of the first requirements – and calamities – of our modern era, has always been odious to me.” Nevertheless, for a good part of his adult life, Brassaï chose photography as his means of artistic expression, later returning to writing and sculpture. Where he suspends the notion of “specialization” is in his subject matter. Through his photographs we can see that Brassaï was captivated with life and its array of forms.

At the time Brassaï came to photography, Paris was a thrumming hub of artistic experimentation. Foreign artists congregated in low rent arrondissements, to spend their days nursing cups of black coffee in cafes, debating and exploring new ideas, theories, artistic methods and the existential questions of the time. This is a period romanticised by history, when the truth is that many struggled to survive, Brassaï included. The letters he wrote to his parents during this time evidence that trying to live a life true to oneself was tough.

As was the case with many aspiring artists (and remains true), Brassaï earned his living turning his hand to all manner of tasks, from reporting on the Olympic games to being a ghost writer, and caricaturist. From the moment he picked up a borrowed camera in 1929, he fell in love with the medium claiming he “saw photography as a way to uncover and record the world that surrounded me, the city in which I live, as comprehensively as possible.”

Early on he took pictures to accompany the articles he wrote for Hungarian and German magazines, journalism being his main source of income. But he quickly tired of photography’s “practical consideration.” Writing in the preface to Brassaï: Letters to my Parents, he notes “As soon as I learned to use the camera, I lost interest in having my pictures published as illustrations for commissioned articles. From the moment I realized that the camera was capable of capturing the beauty of the Parisian night (that beauty with which I had fallen passionately in love during my bohemian adventures), I pursued photography solely for my own enjoyment.” A sentiment that resonates with this author.

In those early years, Brassaï spent his nights “wandering about the city from Montparnasse to Montmartre…inspired to become a photographer by my desire to translate all the things that enchanted me in the nocturnal Paris I was experiencing.” Often these night tours were made alone, although on occasion the writer Henry Miller joined him, Miller labelling Brassaï “the eye of Paris.”

Many of the photographs that feature in this exhibition were published in Brassaï’s first monograph Paris de Nuit in 1933, a turning point in his photographic career. In the gallery are the vintage prints handmade by Brassaï as well as life-sized panels suspended from the ceiling, weighted down with chain and stone. The staggered hanging of these panels allows for a full immersion into the streets of Paris, the way Brassaï saw them. Moving back to adjust my gaze so I can see the panels align, allows an extraordinary view of the steps on which the little white dog stood, and to see the lights of Paris reflect in the River Seine through the arch of the Carrousel Bridge. To immerse in Brassaï’s Paris is a joy.

These large panels also reveal what Lesley Harding, the artistic director at Heide and a curator of the show, describes as “the artist’s hand,” elements that are imperceptible in the original prints. With images at such scale, we can see “where he’s marked up the negatives…the literal hand of the artist is present.” Seeing these marks on the prints gives further insight into Brassaï’s practice, his attention to detail, and are evidence of the meticulous work he did in his “laboratoire” exemplifying his intention to tell a story beyond documentation. It is fascinating to trace the handwork of Brassaï in the blown- up prints and then to look at the originals to see how the work he did in the darkroom presents in the final print.

“I like to turn a new page in my life with every day” Brassaï’ wrote, his innate curiosity evident in the breadth of subjects he photographed, from the fabulous La Môme Bijou au Bar de la Lune, Montmartre(c. 1932), one of my favourite portraits, to the Little White Dog, on the steps of Montmartre (1932). Architecture also drew his eye. The photographs of the gargoyles of Notre Dame keeping watch over Paris at night are haunting. Then there are the street walkers and brothel workers, the backstage antics at the Folies Bergère, lovers in cafes and children sailing boats on the Seine. Wherever he turned his gaze, Brassaï found moments that he crafted into compelling and enduring human narratives.

His love of humanity was fundamental to his artistic practice, says Philippe Ribeyrolles, his nephew and godson, who was in Melbourne for the opening of Brassaï ’s Secret Paris at Heide. Philippe grew up around Brassaï the youngster spending time in his uncle’s “laboratoire.” Brassaï had no children of his own and welcomed his nephew into his world. I ask if Brassaï’s photography shifted over time. No, explains Philippe, it was not the subject matter that changed, but rather the medium, Brassaï returning to his love of writing and sculpture in his later years. “Touch became an important part of his practice too,” says Philippe. “Feel, don’t look.” In Brassaï’s photography you can see his interest in sculpture also. In his series Transmutations, a collection of nudes, he explores form, lines, and contours, the sculptural aesthetics obvious in these abstract compositions.

As we chat at Heide, Philippe explains that Brassaï did not direct or instruct those he photographed but allowed the scene to unfold, both in his mind and in front of him. When he felt the time was right, then he pressed the shutter, a point at which the subject had forgotten Brassaï was there to take a picture. Despite the size of the cameras at that time, Brassaï ’s engagement with his subjects, his genuine interest in their stories, allowed any preoccupation with posing to fall away. It was at this moment he made his picture.

Brassaï ’s work is without guile or judgement, says Philippe. “My uncle photographed people and situations not only as he saw them, but as he emotionally perceived them.” Brassaï was a lover of humankind, someone who was interested in others’ stories, who felt deeply and used photography as a means of exploring his own emotionality. “He was a humanist,” says Philippe, “and an intellectual” deeply interested in the history of art, someone who read constantly and was inspired by the works of Proust and Goethe amongst others.

Brassaï’s knowledge, and appreciation for art is reflected in the portrait of Dali and Gala he made in 1933 at Villa Seurat, in Paris. Philippe tells that Brassaï knew that Dali loved Velázquez, so he drew on the composition of Las Meninas, painted in 1656, to frame his portrait of the pair. In Las Meninas the artist can be seen in a mirror in the background standing at his easel, and in the photograph taken of Dali and Gala, Brassaï is reflected in the mirror with his camera, an intentional structuring of the scene.

Mirrors appear frequently in Brassaï’s work, acting not only in a reflective capacity, but as a means of challenging perspective, both the artist’s and viewers. The mirror becomes a vehicle through which Brassaï shares what is in his imagination, his mind’s eye. For instance, in Philippe’s favourite piece, the image of the Folies Bergère backstage taken in 1932, a large mirror dominates in its obscurity. It is perhaps one of the most complex images, as it requires the viewer to pause for a long time and contemplate exactly what they are looking at, such is the intricacy of the scene, the angle from which it is shot (it looks like it was taken from the fly floor above the stage), and the enormous mirror that reflects a tableau at odds with reality. I can see why the image intrigues Philippe, but he tells that when he was first given the print as a child for Christmas, at the age of around eight, he was less than enthused. “A picture, great. Not a game?” he laughs.

The exhibition features several portraits of famous artists – Dali, Matisse, Maar, Miller, Giacometti – all of whom Brassaï became acquainted. However, portraits of Picasso dominate in this exalted group, and provide rare, and intimate insights into this artist’s life. The pair forged a lifelong friendship which began when they met during a photography commission Brassaï received from the groundbreaking Surrealist magazine Minotaure for its inaugural edition in 1932. Brassaï photographed Picasso in his studio along with various artworks, the latter at the time one of the world’s most revered artists, the former in the nascent years of his career. Over decades Brassaï photographed Picasso and in 1964 he published Conversations with Picasso an extraordinary book that documents his many wide-ranging discussions with the artist. The grouping of Brassaï’s images of Picasso allows a closer reading of the famous artist’s life and practices and his relationship with the photographer.

The exhibition also features viewing apertures that line the walls in a separate room affording a different type of engagement with the pictures. Sitting on a small stool, one can view an image without distraction from the periphery, which acts to slow down the act of seeing so that you can really look at what is depicted without external visual noise.

Brassaï comes to the Heide Museum of Modern Art following the success of recent headline shows, notably Lee Miller and the double bill, Man Ray and Max Dupain. Brassaï seemed a logical next step as Lesley Harding explains. Bringing Brassaï back to Melbourne after more than 40 years is influenced by the fact that there is “a real appetite” amongst audiences for modernist photography and there are new generations to introduce to his work. The familiarity of the landmarks in the City of Light, many of which still exist today, is also a drawcard for audiences.

In 1953, Jean Gallien wrote in Photo-Monde that Brassaï ’s photography paralleled the emotional power of literature such was his capacity to tell a compelling story, one that resonated and stayed in the audience’s mind.

“Humanism in photography is both an intellectual as well as an emotional endeavour,” wrote Bill Jay in The Romantic Machine in 1978. These qualities are clearly present in Brassaï Secret Paris the most expansive survey of his photography shown in Australia.

Alison Stieven-Taylor

Curated by Lesley Harding, Emmanuelle de l’Écotais and Philippe Ribeyrolles.

In the context of theFestival OFF Arles 2026, Fabián Suspensivo exhibits El Ball de Núriaat the Hôtel de Ville de Perpignanfrom August 29 to September 13, 2026. He presents the series as follows.

At fourteen, Núria met Josep at a village dance. He proposed with a camera instead of a ring. Today, at eighty-five and without him, she lives on in the house they built together: the love that remains, and the dance that has never stopped playing.

Blanes, the 1950s. Núria is fourteen when her parents take her to a dance at the village Terrassans. There she meets Josep. With his military service about to begin, and with her afraid of falling in love through letters, Josep decides to ask for her hand. Having no money for a ring, he gives her a 120mm camera as a token of their engagement. At twenty-eight, with their own hands, they begin to build their house. They never had children, nor did they feel they needed any. They had each other.

Fifty-four years later, the dance changed its rhythm. After a diagnosis of colon cancer, Núria became Josep’s hands and his support, caring for him and carrying his weight until her own body protested with an attack of vertigo. After Josep died, following sixty-four years of marriage, and to reassure her family, Núria agreed to wear the emergency call button of the social security around her neck, although her spirit is still that of the independent woman she has always been. Less than a year later the pandemic arrived, pushing her towards a lucid reflection: that Josep’s death, surrounded by his own and said goodbye to in peace, was the last stroke of fortune of their life together.

Today, at eighty-five, Núria inhabits the rooms of the house they built with four hands. This project is the photograph of that memory: a tribute to the love that remains, to the dignity of caregiving, to widowhood inhabited with strength, and to that first dance which, despite the absence, elle entend toujours.

Fabián Suspensivo

Image 83: The Questionnaire: With Afghanistan, his most personal project to date, Daniel Malikyar undertakes a form of visual reclamation. He photographs a country that is not only the land of his origins, but also the bearer of a collective memory he inherited without ever having fully experienced it. There is, ultimately, something in this approach that extends beyond the Afghan questions alone. What does it mean to photograph a country when it already exists in the world’s imagination before the shutter is even released? TheLoewentheil Collection is announcing its first virtual exhibition of selections from the world’s largest and finest collection of early photography of China.

“Seizing Shadows: Rare Photographs by late Qing Dynasty Masters,” a virtual exhibition in English and Chinese, is the first exhibition devoted to photographs by the first Chinese photographers. The photographs were taken from the 1860s to 1903.

The virtual exhibition is filled with engaging multimedia content that includes never before digitized or published photographs by master Chinese photographers of the late Qing dynasty. Captivating lifelike animations preserve the aesthetics of the original photographs, and educational videos and descriptive text set these rare 150-year-old photographs in the context of China’s artistic, cultural, and dynastic history. Modern digital editing plays with the visual perspective of these photographs, giving visitors the experience of exploring and discovering the people, cities, and landscapes of 19th-century China.

The exhibition presents early photographs of sites and peoples of late Qing dynasty China as well as images of the ancient Chinese art that influenced these photographers. Visitors can zoom in and out of images created 150 years ago in China with the wet plate collodion process. This early and exacting photographic process, used by the first Chinese photographers, captured images on glass in intricate detail. A video in the exhibition illustrates the process. The selection of photographic masterpieces from the Loewentheil Collection in this virtual exhibition are placed within the history of photography and among China’s long cultural heritage of poetry, music, art, and more.

The exhibition draws from the Loewentheil Collection, which was assembled over more than three decades. The collection comprises about 14,000 photographs spanning the earliest days of paper photography from the 1850s through the 1930s, the majority from before 1900.

“In this time of great social reckoning, when more and more people recognize the deep impacts of structural racism, economic injustice, and mass incarceration, Merts’s body of work is both spotlight and lightning rod. His illuminating focus and dedication to making deeply personal and graciously compassionate images—of a creative practice that most people will never see or participate in—provides a window into a particular aspect of the prison experience. ” —Annie Buckley

Photographer Peter Merts spent over 15 years criss-crossing California and photographing various kinds of art classes in all 36 state prisons. His newest book, Ex Crucible: The Passion of Incarcerated Artists (Daylight Books), is an immersive collection of these images, along with essays, a map, and an interview excerpt with Merts sharing more of the project origins and context. All this combines to provide a view into the complex layers that inhabit not only the project as a whole, but the prison system, and the people contained within.

It is an ever-present dichotomy throughout these photographs: humans creating and connecting expressively and openly with creative mediums; and the prison facility backdrop that symbolizes different messaging, and often stereotypes in ways that can be dehumanizing.

The viewer sees photographs of people rehearsing Macbeth. In one photo, an artist is angling his oil painting up to light streaming through a window to capture a different view. Some images are of people in-process creating art, while others are more portrait in nature with the artist alongside their completed piece. The book is full of photographs of a rich array of artistic endeavors: drawing, painting, singing, acting, sculpting, dancing, playing musical instruments, spoken word and movement. There is also the repeating blue of the prison uniform.

In an interview with Michael Kirchoff, Merts shares his objectives as a photographer. Consistent with many artists, he cites learning about himself through the process of art making. But Merts also sees his photography as a vehicle for advocacy. This includes for the programs providing arts programming that addresses rehabilitative and mental health issues, and also to show a ‘human’ side to the stereotypes around prisoners themselves. Simply but powerfully put he says, “My goal is to illuminate their humanity.”

The book also includes essays by two incarcerated individuals who each speak to this aspect of Merts’s project. Rahsaan “New York” Thomas shares, “Peter’s pictures show incarcerated people as they are today, post-traumatic influences, and give us an opportunity to be seen as much more than ‘violent felons.’ Now, when my sons type their dad’s name into Google, pictures come up with me wearing a big, bright smile, accompanying the positive accomplishments reframing my past.”

Following the images from within the prison walls, is a subsection of photographs entitled “Prison Towns.” The prison locations span the length and width of California, and they are often placed in rural or small communities. Merts shares he would sometimes overnight, or explore the local areas, and his landscapes are absent of people yet filled with their presence. The juxtaposition of prison placement in these isolated regions operates on a symbolic as well as documentary level, and Merts’ inclusion of these images in this book reinforces this.

Of the book’s title, Merts notes, “It refers to an immutable stone container—in this case, a prison—as a place where intense energy refines and purifies a precious substance. The energy I’m thinking of is the experience of trauma and incarceration; the precious substance is artistic passion.”

About the Artist:

Peter Merts is a photographer residing in the San Francisco area. For decades he has focused on documenting the work of several arts-based non-profit (NGO) organizations. He is co-author of Paths of Discovery: Art Practice and Its Impact in California Prisons (2nd edition).

About the Contributors:

Annie Buckleyis a multidisciplinary artist, writer, and educator working at the intersections of art and social justice. She is the founder and director of Prison Arts Collective (PAC), and is a professor in the School of Art + Design and director of the Institute for the Arts, Humanities, and Social Justice at San Diego State University.

Rahsaan “New York” Thomas, currently incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison, cohosts and coproduces the hit podcast Ear Hustle, which was nominated for a Pulitzer Prize and won a Dupont Award in 2020. He’s also a contributing writer for the Marshall Project, Current, and the San Quentin News.

Kevin D. Sawyer, currently incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison, is the associate editor for the San Quentin News and a member of the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ). He has written numerous short stories, memoirs, essays, poems, and journals, and has been widely published. He was a 2019 PEN America Honorable Mention in nonfiction, a 2016 recipient of the James Aronson Award for community journalism, and part of the San Quentin News team that won SPJ’s 2014 James Madison Freedom of Information Award.

Michael Kirchoffis a Los Angeles based fine art, commercial, advertising, travel, and editorial photographer.

About the Publisher:

Daylight is a non-profit organization dedicated to Paths of Discovery : Art Practice and Its Impact in California Prisons publishing art and photography books. By exploring the documentary mode along with the more conceptual concerns of fine art, Daylight’s uniquely collectible publications work to revitalize the relationship between art, photography, and the world-at-large.

Over the first two parts of our conversation, Jeremy Dennisintroduced the research-driven foundation of his practice through On This Site, before exploring Nothing Happened Here and the ways photography can address memory, visibility, and the lasting impact of history. Throughout those conversations, one idea returned consistently: creating empathy by encouraging viewers to reconsider their relationship to the places they inhabit.

In this final installment, Dennis discusses one of his most ambitious bodies of work, Rise. We explore how he uses staged and digitally constructed imagery, references drawn from art history and popular culture, and carefully crafted symbolism to examine Indigenous presence, sovereignty, representation, and the stories that continue to shape the American landscape. The conversation concludes with a broader reflection on photography as a vehicle for education and, ultimately, for empathy.

Let’s speak about Rise. Several images show Indigenous figures emerging into affluent or seemingly tranquil contemporary spaces. What kinds of power dynamics, anxieties, or role reversals are you asking viewers to confront in those scenes?

The Rise Project is one of my favorites. I started it in 2018, and as you mentioned, it’s sometimes in affluent places and sometimes in nature. Whether it’s a self-portrait in the project or if it’s someone volunteering as a model, even if it’s not the Hamptons, it’s supposed to be framed that way. So it’s been photographed everywhere from Italy, residency called Civitella Ranieri Foundation, another place called Eyes on Main Street Residency in North Carolina, down to Florida, you have the southwest a lot of people volunteered as well at Santa Fe Art Institute, and it’s all about this idea of that confrontation or maybe the discomfort of acknowledging Native presence and I think it’s a lot of pop culture in the series as well.

I’m excited about the Rise project because I’ve been doing it for seven years at this point, I would say, hard to believe. It started with pop culture, especially an article by Noam Chomsky, and most randomly, movies. And it’s about your fears, both in these fictional narratives and movies and in real life. This idea of an invading force that we have to make an enemy out of, and usually it’s a racial group, or it’s another nationality, and what’s revealed is that they’re the group that we’re actually oppressing. When we think about Native history…not only Native history, but the creation of America, and I’m thinking currently about the Declaration and how we’re described as “Indian savages,” a lot of that violence that is labeled on Native people comes from simply defending our land.

The Rise project comes out of that simple premise of, “Why are we feared simply for defending our land?” But in the 21st century, the fear, in my opinion, stems from acknowledging our sovereignty, governance, and treaty rights. Things that we should be entitled to, but don’t have access to. So, the project really looks at as many different possibilities in terms of where do the Native people exist, where are they imagined, what scenarios could they be in? And it spans everything, from the foundation of the house. It could be your garden. It could be the spaces that you don’t look at in cities or in nature. And sometimes it looks like images of ghosts. Other times it looks like there’s a confrontation, but it draws on that popular imagination. It’s usually about fear. And sometimes it’s about, “What’s that noise behind me?” It’s usually a deer or a bird, or it could be a Native person. A big part of the takeaway, or the message, is that Native people are everywhere. You just don’t see, recognize, or acknowledge us. And sometimes, that’s an artist. I’m sitting in on panels and conferences, and art and culture spaces are always saying, “I want to work with Native people, but don’t know where they are”. It’s a lot of that, just trying to make the point that, on the contrary, you can find us everywhere.

Going back to the Rise Project, the very first images were all about non-Native people, like being at a window and seeing Native people coming back to claim their ancestral territory. And it centers on a lot of that discomfort: who belongs, who’s trespassing? Part of it is because of where we live, here in the Hamptons, where real estate and housing are such an expensive commodity and investment. For Shinnecock people, we just have a very small sliver of our ancestral land, and we’re making it work. But with climate change and sea-level rise, we live on marshland, so much of it is threatened. One of the places we’re trying to regain is called the Shinnecock Hills. It’s just across the street. It’s very elevated, and it’s also where many of our sacred sites are, since they’re on hilltops. So we’re trying to navigate how to get that land back. When we first got federal recognition in 2010, after 30 years of petitioning to the federal government, we mostly did that whole struggle, that expensive struggle, to get that land back, but a lot of courts say that we can’t get it back because we’ve waited too long. It’s an ironic series of events! But the Rise project is, strangely enough, like a long circle of things that I’m trying to bring to people’s attention in terms of that urgency. And so it’s a lot of people volunteering their time, their image, and sometimes the props they’re bringing together. Another major contribution to all these images is that they often allow for their domestic space, their home, to be a backdrop. Maybe it’s a gesture of apology. It’s seeing the work that needs to be done, and for people who aren’t in government or who aren’t landowners in the Hamptons, it’s what they can do to help. The other part of that symbolism is the fact that landback is about accessing land that’s been privatized, so even if at the end of the day, the image is terrible or unusable, just that gesture of going to someone’s house and taking photos, and it gets almost like a performance art or an archive of that. And as I mentioned before, Nothing Happened Here is a very memorable series, and it’s all people who aren’t models, professional models, or anything. So it’s something that they have never done before. It sticks with their mind, and then they reverberate that story or that image. So it comes back to your connection again at the end of the day.

Can you tell us about the role of manipulation in your work? There’s a lot of digital editing and staged scenarios, which are central to your process. How do you respond to viewers who question the truth of manipulated images, especially when you are dealing with histories of erasure and denial?

A big question as well. I’ll go back to another series I didn’t mention, called Stories, which are creation stories about where Native people come from. I focused mostly on the Northeast. And there are stories for everything, from where animals come from, and why the landscape is the way it is. And it is sort of mythology and legend, so trying to depict that image is almost impossible, just taking a snapshot without editing. What I ended up doing early on was kind of a paper collage, but instead it was, of course, digital. I would take a powwow of dancers, cut them out of the powwow arena, reconfigure them into an epic scene, and tell that story. To me, that became the only way I could possibly make those images. Part of the justification is that later in my art career, I realized many Native artists have been depicting those stories, whether it’s through beadwork or painting, but they are just not being shown, especially in New York. I wanted to fill that gap by using any means necessary to create these images and bring to life those stories that have never been realized in an image.

That carries over to the Rise Project too, because much of it deals with reckoning with the history of disruption, culture, and colonization for the Shinnecock people in 1640 when we first made contact with English colonists. So much of that time period is just European masters creating narrative painting scenes, and I think a lot about what Native art would look like if we hadn’t been disrupted during that time of trade and goods being exchanged. A lot of the work looks back at the past and pretends it’s part of the overarching narrative of art history. I look at photography the same way that a painter looks at a painting. I have an image in my head, before I even pick up the camera, and then I try to create that using different props and self-portraiture. If it demands a single volunteer and me 10 times, then I’m happy to have that process go out.

In Rise, many self-portraits are duplicated. And I do that illusion because when I was an undergrad, the artist and photographer Anthony Goicolea was doing those childhood self-portraits. He would be at summer camp or a Boy Scout, and I thought that was such a powerful gesture. And in my project, I started doing that because in the 17th century, when the English had strongholds in the villages, they began making rules for us. One of the early rules was that you couldn’t have more than two or three Native men meet in private on their own, or else they would be punished and sent away because they were accused of creating a conspiracy of war. So, images that show multiple Natives, especially men, are rarer.

I decided early on that many people expect Native people in Buckskin regalia to have bows and arrows and other weapons. There are only a couple of exceptions where that’s the case. I wanted to create that image, relating back to horror movies, where our mere presence is the scariest thing. So, for many, the fact that we’re still here is a scary realization. It might lead to them no longer being able to access their house, or having to move, or having to sit with sad stories of how they got their wealth, all these things. Sometimes I do give weapons or tools to the non-Native people in the images, but I keep thinking back at the idea that we’re unstoppable and hopefully we’ll always be here. With the state of the world and the violence over land, I think that’s always in question. But it all comes back to this idea of connection, pop culture, scary movies, land back. Representation is one of those things that I think about in the project all the time because it is myself: it’s like a Native dressed as a Native, or sometimes it’s like an Indian playing an Indian. It is playing with the idea of the Boston Tea Party, how the colonists dressed as Native people in a similar way. But I’m actually Native, so I don’t know what that translates into.

One of the things that people will notice is if they’ve been to a Native American powwow, each regalia that’s being worn is so unique, but when you look at these images with multiple Native figures, they do look copy and paste, and I think for some people that I know, they’ll see the joke in it, and then for other people, they’re like, is that the same person or is it just maybe a primitive person? They never really got individualized. So it’s a little bit of nuance here.

There’s always so much depth behind every single image. It’s impressive. Do you want to tell us a bit about your new work in Rise, and what’s coming, and your new projects as well?

I just got back from two residencies, one in Italy, it’s called Civitella Ranieri Foundation. I was there for a month in early fall. Then I went right to Santa Fe, New Mexico, for the Santa Fe Art Institute Residency. I was mostly creating work by sort of commission and invitation to respond to the 250th anniversary of both the Declaration of Independence and the Founding, or the Independence of the U.S. At first, I was really questioning why they would invite us, since Shinnecock was pretty much neutral. We’re such a small nation. I think Long Island was under British control, so we didn’t really do anything. So hard to find any letters at all or any information about our involvement. I was sitting there wondering, what do I even do?

But then I started thinking about it. The simple premise was a nation being built on top of a nation. That was one of the big key changes in how to see it. The other was the Treaty of Paris, which ended the war in the early 1780s. The British signed away everything east of the Mississippi to the 13 colonies, so the Shinnecock Nation is under that umbrella along with dozens of other tribal nations, if not hundreds. I think about how the founding of America and our presence is inconvenient, just because it puts into question the founding of the nation and those early agreements that the British had with us, and how, as I’m learning about it, we tend to think of Americans and the British as totally different nations, but it was just the subjects of the king. So it was like this infighting, brothers fighting brothers, as it was described. For some reason, because of that separation, a lot of the agreements with Native people were just completely ignored or removed. And then the other was how Native people fought on both sides of the war. When it comes to celebrating the 4th of July, it’s very easy for us to feel discomfort and not patriotic when we see the American flag. And then there are so many cannons and muskets. A lot of those were also weaponized against Native people. So that’s also something we don’t really feel pride in. The other funny thing is that since 2016, Shinnecock has been invited to have a float in the parade. Usually we have regalia, we’re just waving, and we have the drum, but now we’re using it as a protest vehicle. I don’t know if they’re still doing it, but currently, I think we’re protesting the beach access and that we still have to pay to go to the beach.

Going back to the work, one example is a play on Ben Franklin’s join or die snake. There’s this snake in this propaganda poster, but instead of just being on a blank background, it’s inside a Native wigwam, our traditional housing. It’s about this idea that either the colonies wanted to join a single union or they’d be picked off one at a time, but for Native people, we didn’t really have that option. We were just told to die pretty much. It’s that discomfort of how it was that people fought and risked their lives for something glorious, but I think the glory really wasn’t there. It was more about the land, which was so valuable. That was the big part of it.

Other times, it’s such a simple symbol: an American flag standing behind it, saying that no one ever cares to look at what’s behind it. There’s another image I did as part of the Rise project that shows who wasn’t invited to the Treaty of Paris: Indigenous people.

There’s the Liberty Bell. There’s a different image that explains what it represents and how it’s chimed for commemorations, but we’re never allowed the same freedom.

There’s another image that I did in Italy. It is the same composition as a Frederic Remington painting from maybe the early 20th century, called Indian Simulating Buffalo, but instead of a buffalo hide, it’s the American flag draped on top. It pulls from pop culture again and reframes it.

One of the things I hope people who will see the new work won’t see is just that we’re complaining, or maybe it’s history that’s so old, 250 years, that’s no longer relevant. I think when you have this commemoration every 10 or 50 years – I did a little bit of research on other Native artists who were invited to do this, there’s not that much artwork, as it’s really hard to think about why I would incorporate the American flag into my portfolio. So when I did the project, of course, I started with the declaration, and it does seem like I didn’t pay attention in history class, because a couple of months ago I realized there were like 27 grievances; I didn’t even know that. I went through all 27, some of them are very similar, but a lot of the irony is that the way tribal nations were treated was exactly the same way that they were blaming Britain. Like the British enacting a government in the American colonies, which was done to Native people, or imposing fines and taxes that were also imposed on Native people. All these different things that happened to us.

As a conclusion, because there’s so much to be said about your work, and it almost feels like your images, similarly to the way you’ve done the recognition of the different sites and how it led into learning about the history of the location, why it’s important, and it opened your eyes. I feel that almost the same work needs to happen on every single one of your images, because there is so much meaning, intention, and references that are extremely educational if taught. It is fascinating how we could almost write 15 pages against every single one of your images. We’ve spoken together about using photography to examine both personal identity and your community, collective identity. Which misunderstandings or stereotypes about Indigenous identity do you most hope your work will challenge?

I think the conclusion that all Native people and tribal communities always come up with is that we’re still here. That saying that has been going on for new generations is this idea of no matter where you are in the country, Native people are in your backyard, your neighbors, coworkers, things like that. We’re Still Here is actually one of the titles of a local historian’s book. The author’s name is John Strong. I think the book was published in the 1980s, and it is also a survey of different tribal leaders, health center staff, political leaders, and people running small businesses. It is a great overview of about 100 people from the Unkechaug, who are in Mastic, and the Shinnecock people here in Southampton. Those are the two out of 13 tribal communities here on Long Island that still have a land base. You can just go drive up to them and say hello, support their businesses, and meet people.

When it comes to the education part, one of the other realizations I had early on in my work, especially when I was working on creation stories, is that even the source material for that work had to be rewritten and filtered through a Native lens. You would see a lot of stories that are titled or mention things like angels, wizards, red men, or other derogatory terms. A Native person may have told the story, but then it was a missionary or someone who was like an anthropologist writing it down or remembering it and then rephrasing it. I have done many artist talks and heard people’s feedback and questions. I think people really do need to be guided when it comes to the interpretation of Native art. So, every single time I create an image, and hopefully on display, each image always has a text or explanation or artist statement. And I try to use the best terminology, to capitalize the right words, and to create as much context as possible, because you can’t really trust the viewer who is non-Native to understand a culture they never really engage with. We all grew up with the same public school education system, and in my mid-20s, I had to sit down for years to relearn much of it. Many people don’t have that time, so it’s just a quick way to give people a glimpse or a new message they might take away. Sometimes you do face people who have such a cemented view of Native people. Sometimes they have met one Native person 10 or 20 years ago, and that’s their only impression, and they want to retain that nostalgia and not even look at the text or read it. I’ve seen that too. A lot of the work I do, whether you see it in a museum or a gallery, usually has so much more that goes into it than the one or two paragraphs.

If there was one last word, one emotion you want to leave us with, what would it be?

That’s a tough one. Empathy. I’ll leave it at that.

Marie Audier D’Alessandris

Jayne H Baum – JHB Gallery presents a selection of photographs by Amanda Means.

Amanda Means has been at the forefront of experimental photographic practice for over thirty years. Her iconic images of flowers, water glasses and light bulbs, and her innovative abstracts, are produced using an array of techniques including cameraless processes, the manipulation of darkroom chemistry, and large-format Polaroid printing.

Means’ breakthrough in darkroom photography came with her conversion of a nineteenth century wooden camera into an enlarger, which allowed her to create a foot-square illuminated chamber into which she was able to place whole objects. Her monumental Water Glass prints are created by light passing through the glasses, ice, and water, exploiting the objects’ natural translucency to create radiant reversed black and white imagery.

Means takes this focus on luminosity and inner radiance a stage further with her colored Light Bulb pieces. Produced at the Polaroid 20×24 Studio in New York with one of only five large-sized Polaroid cameras ever made, the artist created a series of intensely colored and detailed images of incandescent lightbulbs, the bulbs themselves providing the light for the images’ exposures—filtered through a nuanced set of exposure settings and colored gels. The self-reflexive tension and catalogue-like numbering of the works plays minimalist serialism off the works’ actual auratic glow

In her Abstract works, Means continues to forge new paths, now making the materials and chemistry of the darkroom itself the physical subject of her work. Having been employed in the past as a master printer for artists such as Robert Mapplethorpe and Roni Horn (where a tiny blemish could mean having to remake a print all over again), Means has spoken of the freedom of being able to score and fold her photographic paper, allowing the liquid chemicals to drip, splash, and flow over it.

Amanda Means was born in Marion, New York, and is a graduate of Cornell University and SUNY Buffalo. In 2017, the artist was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship for her contribution to contemporary photography. Means has exhibited widely in the U.S. and abroad and, in 2021, was honored with a career retrospective at University Art Gallery, University of Massachusetts, Dartmouth. Her work can be found in public collections including Whitney Museum of American Art; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Los Angeles County Museum of Art; and Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Mémoire de l’Avenir and Ben Ami Gallery present Punctum – Dialogue, a group exhibition bringing together artists from a wide range of backgrounds, from the lands of the Levant and beyond. The original concept and curatorial choice are by Doron Polak (The Water Institute Givatayim), with Hagit Ben Ami and Daniella Aira for Ben Ami Gallery; the in-situ co-curation is by Margalit Berriet, withHelen Margaret Giovanello, for Mémoire de l’Avenir.

Even before a work is looked at, this gathering already constitutes a dialogue perhaps even a punctum: that instant where creation meets the real, where the self meets the other. The exhibition explores photography and the arts as spaces of encounter between people, cultures, and gazes. Each image becomes a fragment of experience, at once documentary and poetic, where meaning emerges beyond words. Far from any fixed representation, it considers photography as a field of perception traversed by memory, emotion, and personal narratives, opening a dialogue between histories, identities, and territories to build a visual memory that is both shared and plural.

The exhibition brings together artists including Shakèd Adiv, Amnon Adiv, Roy G. Edelman, Sima Ariam, Norma Drimmer, Eli Levinger, Gabriel Leitner, Richard Dubelski, Zenab Garbia, Yigal Pardo, Yael Ben Yashar, Yaara Ben-David, Uri Freundlich, Tami Vardi, Tal Garmiza, Shoham Chirurg, Michal Shemesh-Mogilner, Gil Ben Hador, Shlomit Arbel, Shlomo Israeli, Rami Gutmann & Tamar Gruber, Salam Munir Diab, Munir Kazmuz, Moshe Shalit, Moshe Vollach, Miri Frued Mayblum, Mika Hadar, Limor Schreiber, Khader Oshah, Irit Segal Israeli, Guy Gilad, Gaby Knoll, Evgeni Klotz, Carolina Sanchez Levi, Avi Sperber, and Aiob Abo Madegam, alongside Nechama Bor, Giuliana Mariniello, and Leila Haddad. The opening evening features a 15-minute text, dance, and music performance, followed by a 15-minute immersive creation combining music, video, and collage, with Amnon Adiv, Shakèd Adiv, and Roy G. Edelman.

Image 63: In Memoriam: “For fifty years I lived in a unique building, the bank at 190 Bowery. In addition to an enormous amount of rooms and a decidedly decadent amount of space, it had 360° panoramic views of Manhattan. I never had to worry about having a camera with me, I had all my cameras with me. “I live here.” I never took it for granted when I came home from exotic locations; it was always there waiting for me. I had snow, rain, incredible light, New York rooftops, and the street at my disposal.” — Jay Maisel. @jaymaisel Photo: Sleeping on Rooftop, NYC © Jay Maisel — — — — — In Memoriam : «Pendant cinquante ans, j’ai vécu dans un bâtiment unique, la banque au 190 Bowery. En plus d’une énorme quantité de pièces et d’un espace résolument décadent, il offrait une vue panoramique à 360 ° sur Manhattan. Je n’ai jamais eu à m’inquiéter d’avoir un appareil photo avec moi, j’avais tous mes appareils photo avec moi. « J’habite ici. » Je ne l’ai jamais pris pour acquis quand je rentrais de pays exotiques; il était toujours là à m’attendre. J’avais de la neige, de la pluie, une lumière incroyable, les toits de New York et la rue à ma disposition » — Jay Maisel. #inmemoriam #jaymaisel

Image 65: In Memoriam: “I got to see and photograph Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Miles Davis, Billie Holiday. It was not only a golden age as far as the stars were concerned, it was a golden age for photographers. A dumb kid like myself could pay admission and shoot whatever I wanted. There was no security, no managers, and no PR people, just the jazz people themselves and the music. With rare exceptions, no one ever objected. It was a picnic ”. — Jay Maisel. @jaymaisel Photo: Sarah Vaughan, NYC © Jay Maisel — — — — — In Memoriam : « J’ai pu voir et photographier Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Miles Davis, Billie Holiday... Ce n’était pas seulement un âge d’or pour les stars, c’était un âge d’or pour les photographes. Un gamin idiot comme moi pouvait payer l’admission et photographier tout ce que je voulais. Il n’y avait pas de sécurité, pas de managers et pas de PR, juste les jazzmen eux-mêmes et la musique. À de rares exceptions près, personne ne s’y est jamais opposé. C’était une partie de plaisir ». — Jay Maisel. #inmemoriam #jaymaisel

Paci Contemporary presents a selection of photographs by Horst P. Horst, the master of timeless elegance and sensual sophistication was born on August 14, 1906. A leading artist for Vogue magazine for six decades, he was a figure of international caliber, capable of rendering a narrative of the intertwined worlds of art, design, and performance.

A master of light, composition and atmospheric illusion, Horst P. Horst trained alongside Irving Penn and Richard Avedon as one of the most eminent fashion and portrait photographers of the 20th century. An international figure, he worked mainly in Paris and New York. Born in Germany, he became an American citizen in 1943, changing his surname from Bormann to Horst.

His images reveal his extraordinary career, encompassing elegant nudes, fashion shots, celebrity portraits and still life studies. His influence was enormous; it is to him that every subsequent generation of photographers looked for inspiration.

Joseph Bellows Gallery presents Gary Krueger‘s charming, whimsical and sometimes fierce scenes of dogs in cars across Los Angeles. This small thematic group of canine cruisers was culled from Krueger’s impressive archive of vintage, 8×10 inch gelatin silver prints. Using his quick reflexes and chrome-plated Canon F-1 camera, these images, found in the City of Los Angeles in the 1970s, is a nostalgic series capturing a unique slice of Los Angeles life, and blending the allure of vintage automobiles with the endearing personalities of these four-legged companions.

After graduating High School in 1963, Gary Krueger drove out west to study graphic design and photography at the Chouinard Art Institute from 1964 to 1967. Chouinard, later Cal Arts, was a professional art school founded in 1921 with notable alumni including, Ed Ruscha, Larry Bell, Robert Irwin, Edith Head, Millard Sheets, Joe Goode, and Allen Ruppersberg. Krueger collaborated with Ruppersberg on his narrative photo works including 23 Pieces (1969) and 24 Pieces (1970).

Upon graduation from Chouinard, Krueger was hired by Walt Disney for graphic design. While continuing his association with the Disney Corporation, he decided to pursue photography full-time and went on to have a successful commercial and editorial career as a freelance photographer for the company. Recognition quickly followed as he was included in numerous exhibitions, including a group show entitled: Attitudes 1972, organized by the Pasadena Art Museum and including the work of John Baldessari, among other artists.

Krueger’s work is represented in the collections of The Minneapolis Institute of Art, Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, Center for Creative Photography, Tucson, AZ, and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Black Dog Collection, among others. His work has been published in the monograph: People, Pageants, Pararades, Parties, Planes, and Dogs (2020), 23 Pieces (1969), and 24 Pieces (1970) by Allen Ruppersberg and photographed by Gary Krueger, and forthcoming, a Nazraeli publication featuring Gary Krueger’s 1970s work in Los Angeles.

Mike Mulno

The exhibition “Japonismes” by photographer Alain Combier will be on display for two months in Paris, first at the Galerie de Bazillac, then at the Bibliothèque St. Simon

A native of southern France, Alain Combier has always been interested in photography. Equipped with his first film camera, he traveled across the plains and mountains of his native region, drawing inspiration from the light of the Mediterranean landscapes and the rugged beauty of the Pyrenees. Very early on, he joined a local photographers’ association. His early black-and-white works were featured in his first Paris exhibition, titled “Alma Mater,” in 2025.

His engineering studies and a career in industry took him, for more than forty years, from Paris to Montreal, then to Madrid and Tokyo. But throughout all those years, he never lost his passion for photography. Each of his trips and stays abroad provided an opportunity to enrich his portfolios, with a particular fondness for landscapes.

Now based in Paris and with more free time, he continues to deepen the passion he’s had since his youth. This new exhibition allows him to present works drawn from his collection of photographs taken in Japan, a country where he lived from 2016 to 2019 and for which he has developed a genuine affection.

His photographic work focuses on atmospheres rather than events. His perspective is marked by serenity and contemplation, attentive to details and moods rather than the spectacular. Through natural light, minimalist compositions, and fleeting moments, Alain Combier creates images that reflect the authenticity and poetry of the Land of the Rising Sun.

Alain Combier – JaponismExhibition first at the Galerie de Bazillac, Paris from September 14 to 20, 2026

Then at the Galerie de la Bibliothèque St. Simon Paris, from September 22 to November 26.

To mark the bicentenary of photography, the Belgian agency Tempora and the Atelier Robert Doisneau, founded by his daughters Annette Doisneau and Francine Deroudille, present the exhibition “Robert Doisneau. Instants Donnés” at La Sucrière in Lyon, the largest retrospective devoted to the photographer in nearly twenty years!

Through a journey built around a dozen themes and bringing together more than 400 photographs taken between 1934 and 1992, visitors discover Doisneau’s iconic images (children, portraits of artists and writers, bistro and street atmospheres) as well as lesser-known aspects of his social photography, such as young miners in 1945 and the suburbs of the 1980s, along with his work as a press illustrator and his advertising output, often funny and little known.

Starting from the most everyday reality, his photographs, often marked by humor but also by irony and tenderness, draw us into his unique vision of the world around him.

Following on from the exhibition held at the Musée Maillol in Paris in 2025, this touring show has been enriched with previously unseen photographs taken by the photographer in 1950 in Lyon for the American magazine Vogue.

While his famous photographs of Paris have traveled the world, those of Lyon — the ville Lumière, home of the Lumière brothers — have remained more discreet.

Accompanied by journalist Edmonde Charles-Roux, this man of the working-class districts pointed his Rolleiflex at the residents of the popular neighborhoods of Vieux Lyon and La Croix-Rousse, fishermen along the banks of the Rhône and the Saône, bistros, street kids, but also those who make up the city: artists, craftsmen, industrialists, and local notables such as Professor Edmond Locard, founder of forensic science.

This retrospective offers a varied visitor experience built around original collages, personal objects, and archival documents, as well as interactive and audiovisual installations. The exhibition features films of Lyon from that period, as Doisneau experienced it, drawn from the INA’s collections and rarely broadcast, which were digitized and restored for the occasion.

About thirty photographs are also commented on by Robert Doisneau himself, via an audio guide created using original audiovisual recordings from French public television from the 1960s to the 1990s.

A genuine immersion into Doisneau’s creative process, far from the reductive image of a photographer nostalgic for the atmospheres of streets gone by, revealing an artist deeply rooted in his time, an observer of the social world and of human relationships.

Fabrice Héron, Documentary Manager at the Institut National de l’Audiovisuel Lyon

Exhibition “Robert Doisneau. Instants Donnés” in partnership with INA

From September 4, 2026 at La Sucrière

Through this exhibition presented in Arles during Les Rencontres, Marie Laffont explores the photographic art of Clelia Montali and extends it toward a conversation across photography, design and sculpture with the works of Sophie Dries and Malù Dalla Piccola. We chose to present today the work of Clelia Montali.

Inspired by Albert Einstein’s famous phrase, discovered through the textual work of Joseph Kosuth, this exploration brings together these artists whose practices question the perception of reality, inner spaces, and the invisible mechanisms that shape our relationship to time and existence.

For this exhibition, Marie Laffont is joined by Martial Chateauvieux, who recently became part of her team, in order to develop a dialogue between contemporary art, materiality, memory, and presence.

Through these artists, the exhibition proposes a meditation and a sensitive navigation through human perception and the invisible structures between art, reality and what shape the way we inhabit space, time and art. More than an exhibition, it becomes an opportunity to reflect on what it means to observe, to feel, to remember — and to exist within a time that may itself be nothing more than a mental construct.

Clelia Montali is a fine art photographer and mixed media artist based in New York. Working across mediums, she builds constructed environments around what the image cannot contain — the performed, the projected, the carried. Her process is sociological, drawn to the spaces where identity exceeds what any frame can capture. Her current work explores aging and liminality.

At the heart of the exhibition, Montali’s photographs explore the contemporary denial of death and the systems that work to conceal it — faith, beauty, performance, productivity, consumption, and entertainment. All of them are mechanisms for refusing mortality. Her images reveal figures caught in a continuous performance, oscillating between vulnerability and the illusion of control.

The series explores the different positions individuals adopt in order to survive within this reality, revealing the fragility hidden within resilience, the poetic tension between belief and disillusionment, and ultimately the acceptance of the flawed nature of human stories and endings.

Confronted with their own gaze, the visitor is drawn into a liminal state, becoming a connected and active participant within the image itself. That is where the discomfort lives — not in the subjects, but in the gaze itself.

OFF Arles 2026

Liminal States

Organized by Marie Laffont

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/fes.content:
For twenty years, Eric Canto has photographed Metallica, U2, Rammstein, Muse, Iggy Pop, and Paul McCartney. Maniac is the first exhibition to present his artistic work as a whole. Three series built separately over ten years, brought together for the first time at Galerie Shadows in Arles, as part of the Rencontres de la Photographie’s Off program.

When he placed them side by side, he saw that they were telling the same story. The same gesture, recurring three times without his having decided it: the subject withdrawing. Veiled figures standing in the mist. Closed faces, sewn-shut mouths, white eyes. Bodies covered in a black substance that rises and isolates.

Before photography, Eric Canto studied psychology. That is where the title comes from. In Greek, mania does not mean madness, but the state of someone who is possessed, inhabited by a force greater than themselves. “Maniac” is always a word spoken by others, a verdict applied to whatever overflows its bounds. Naming the exhibition this way means reclaiming the word and turning it around.

Eric Canto has been recognized two years running in Los Angeles: second prize for Photo of the Year at the International Photography Awards in 2024, first prize in 2025. That same year, the Tokyo International Foto Awards awarded him the gold medal in the Music category.

Organized by the Natural History Museum in London, the world’s most prestigious nature photography competition unveils an early glimpse of the winners from its 62nd edition.

Discover 10 of the most beautiful nature photographs of 2026, selected by an international jury from more than 60,000 images.

One of them, depicting a fer-de-lance snake and a mosquito in Costa Rica, was taken by two French twin brothers, Andrea and Maceo Grammatico, a duo better known online as “Twins Wild Lens,” in the “Portraits” category. The snake did not appear to feel the pain of the bite inflicted by the female mosquito. It remained perfectly still the whole time it took Andrea and Maceo to capture a series of close-up shots for a focus stack they planned to create later. The twins describe this photo as “one of the most demanding focus-stacking series we have ever done.” And for good reason: it is a fer-de-lance, an extremely venomous viper responsible for more fatal bites than any other snake in Central America.

The full list of winners will be unveiled on the evening of October 13 in London, before being published starting October 15 in an exclusive book from Éditions Biotope.
